**For workspaces operating with air freight as primary transport mode**

*Operational implication:* The 41% year-on-year spot rate increase to $3.40/kg (May 2026) and 35% full-market rate increase to $3.23/kg (week 21) represent the direct cost exposure for any shipment booked at current spot. For high-value, time-sensitive cargo verticals where air is the primary mode — fine art, live events equipment, luxury goods, high-value automotive components, humanitarian — this rate environment compresses margin on contracts priced before March 2026.

COST ALERT

*Analytical inference:* Workspaces that secured long-term contracted rates before April 2026 are temporarily insulated; however, long-term rates peaked at end of April and will reset at renewal. Any contract renewing in Q3 2026 will be benchmarked against a market still 22%+ above year-ago levels on the long-term index.

**Jet fuel surcharges — pass-through discipline required**

*Operational implication:* Jet fuel prices rose 121.1% year-on-year in April 2026. Carriers maintaining emergency fuel surcharges will pass these through. For cargo verticals where the workspace acts as freight forwarder (not cargo principal), the pass-through mechanics — whether surcharges are included in the contracted rate or itemised separately — directly determine margin exposure. IATA's Director General cited "elevated operating costs" as the central sustainability test for coming months. *Source: IATA, "Air Cargo Demand Up 4.0% in April Amid Middle East Disruption," 28 May 2026. https://www.iata.org/en/pressroom/2026-releases/05-28-air-cargo-demand-up-april-middle-east-disruption/

**Gulf corridor-routing impact by trade lane**

Gulf-linked corridors in scope for the workspace's Americas–Europe–Asia trade lanes:

- Europe–Middle East: -25.9% YoY CTK in April 2026, 2 consecutive months of contraction. *Source: IATA, "Air Cargo Demand Up 4.0% in April Amid Middle East Disruption," 28 May 2026. https://www.iata.org/en/pressroom/2026-releases/05-28-air-cargo-demand-up-april-middle-east-disruption/
- Middle East–Asia: -22.4% YoY CTK in April 2026, 2 consecutive months of contraction. *Source: IATA, "Air Cargo Demand Up 4.0% in April Amid Middle East Disruption," 28 May 2026. https://www.iata.org/en/pressroom/2026-releases/05-28-air-cargo-demand-up-april-middle-east-disruption/
- Asia–Europe: +16.2% YoY, 38 consecutive months of growth. This corridor is absorbing diverted demand and remains the most active alternative routing. *Source: IATA, "Air Cargo Demand Up 4.0% in April Amid Middle East Disruption," 28 May 2026. https://www.iata.org/en/pressroom/2026-releases/05-28-air-cargo-demand-up-april-middle-east-disruption/
- Asia–North America: +8.3% YoY, 6 consecutive months of growth. *Source: IATA, "Air Cargo Demand Up 4.0% in April Amid Middle East Disruption," 28 May 2026. https://www.iata.org/en/pressroom/2026-releases/05-28-air-cargo-demand-up-april-middle-east-disruption/

*Operational implication:* Any shipment routing through Dubai, Sharjah, or Gulf-hub connections faces materially higher risk of delay or diversion. Workspaces with standing routings through Emirates or Etihad connections should confirm current operational status before booking.

**E-commerce and low-value cargo**

China's low-value and e-commerce exports fell 11% year-on-year in April 2026, marking a fifth consecutive monthly decline. Shipments to the United States dropped 33%, while exports to Europe and Asia Pacific recorded smaller declines. *Source: Xeneta / Stat Times, "Global air cargo spot rates surge 41% in May amid tensions," 6 June 2026. https://www.stattimes.com/air-cargo/global-air-cargo-spot-rates-surge-41-in-may-amid-tensions-1359396

*Operational implication:* For workspaces handling any China-origin air freight to the US, the e-commerce volume collapse removes a portion of belly-cargo co-loading that previously helped absorb fixed costs. The EU de minimis removal from 1 July 2026 adds a further structural headwind to China-origin small-parcel air volumes.

**Multimodal option — Sea-Air**

Flexport has launched Sea-Air Express, a multimodal solution for shippers looking to circumvent Middle East disruptions, delivering cargo from Asia to Europe in as few as 27 days, at rates up to 41% below pure air freight. *Source: Flexport, "Middle East Escalation Disrupts Global Ocean and Air Freight Networks," updated 2 June 2026. https://www.flexport.com/blog/middle-east-escalation-disrupts-global-ocean-and-air-freight-networks/

*Analytical inference:* For workspace cargo verticals where 27-day transit is acceptable (not live events, not humanitarian emergency aid, but potentially some luxury goods and automotive components), Sea-Air represents a cost-reduction lever while Gulf air capacity remains suppressed. This is a named competitor move that changes the competitive benchmark for Asia-Europe proposals.

---

**Who benefits in the current market**

*Analytical inference:* Forwarders with confirmed contracted capacity on Asia-Europe and transpacific lanes — the two corridors showing the strongest YoY demand growth — hold a competitive advantage over those relying on spot market access. Capacity constraint is the differentiating factor, not rate-finding.

*Analytical inference:* Operators with dedicated freighter relationships or block-space agreements on non-Gulf routing (particularly Asia-Europe at +16.2% YoY demand) are positioned to offer service reliability that spot-dependent competitors cannot match.

**Who is exposed**

*Analytical inference:* Workspaces or competitors heavily routing through Gulf hubs — relying on Emirates SkyCargo or Etihad Cargo as primary belly-cargo or freighter partners — face both higher rates and lower reliability. The named data points confirm Gulf carriers' capacity is still 22.9% below YoY in April and Gulf capacity remains at barely half pre-war levels as of week 21.

*Analytical inference:* Competitors whose pricing to clients was built on 2025 rate benchmarks for Gulf-routing lanes will either be absorbing large fuel surcharge losses or renegotiating client contracts under unfavorable conditions.

**Flexport's Sea-Air Express**

Flexport has named its Sea-Air Express as a direct market response to Middle East disruptions. This is a concrete competitive move by a named, large forwarder. *Source: Flexport, "Middle East Escalation Disrupts Global Ocean and Air Freight Networks," updated 2 June 2026. https://www.flexport.com/blog/middle-east-escalation-disrupts-global-ocean-and-air-freight-networks/ The product offers Asia-to-Europe transit in 27 days at rates up to 41% below pure air freight. *Industry interpretation:* This represents a named competitor's attempt to convert the air capacity gap into a multimodal upsell — a commercial posture the workspace should evaluate against its own service architecture.

**Transpacific corridor: AI-driven demand**

Artificial intelligence-related shipments, particularly semiconductors and data centre equipment, continued to drive strong transpacific demand. *Source: Xeneta / Stat Times, "Global air cargo spot rates surge 41% in May amid tensions," 6 June 2026. https://www.stattimes.com/air-cargo/global-air-cargo-spot-rates-surge-41-in-may-amid-tensions-1359396 *Analytical inference:* Workspaces with established transpacific lane coverage for technology cargo verticals are positioned on the highest-demand corridor currently operating.

---

**Geopolitical actors**

The U.S. military and Iranian forces are the principal parties to the conflict whose exchanges have directly triggered airspace closures and fuel price spikes. U.S. forces struck Iranian radar and drone control sites on Goruk and Qeshm Island after a U.S. drone was shot down over international waters; Iran's IRGC responded by firing ballistic missiles at U.S. forces in Kuwait. *Source: Flexport, "Middle East Escalation Disrupts Global Ocean and Air Freight Networks," updated 2 June 2026. https://www.flexport.com/blog/middle-east-escalation-disrupts-global-ocean-and-air-freight-networks/

Trump convened his national security team on 29 May 2026 to make a "final determination" on a ceasefire framework, but the meeting ended without a decision. *Source: Flexport, "Middle East Escalation Disrupts Global Ocean and Air Freight Networks," updated 2 June 2026. https://www.flexport.com/blog/middle-east-escalation-disrupts-global-ocean-and-air-freight-networks/

**Airlines and capacity holders**

Freighter operations by Gulf-based carriers have largely recovered, although passenger services are not expected to fully return until conflict conditions stabilise and traveller confidence improves. *Source: WorldACD / Stat Times, "Global air cargo tonnage, pricing and capacity decline in early May," 18 May 2026. https://www.stattimes.com/amp/air-cargo/global-air-cargo-tonnage-pricing-and-capacity-decline-in-early-may-1359159

Rising fuel costs have also led airlines to reduce or cancel unprofitable routes, particularly regional services operated by narrowbody aircraft, although the impact on cargo capacity has remained limited. *Source: WorldACD / Stat Times, "Global air cargo tonnage, pricing and capacity decline in early May," 18 May 2026. https://www.stattimes.com/amp/air-cargo/global-air-cargo-tonnage-pricing-and-capacity-decline-in-early-may-1359159

*Analytical inference:* Non-Gulf carriers — particularly Asia-Pacific and European operators — are the primary beneficiaries of diverted cargo flows, as they hold the capacity that Gulf-linked carriers have withdrawn, and their pricing power increases as the capacity gap remains.

With dedicated freighters carrying much of the growth, air cargo is once again keeping supply chains moving amid trade disruptions, per IATA's Director General. *Source: IATA, "Air Cargo Demand Up 4.0% in April Amid Middle East Disruption," 28 May 2026. https://www.iata.org/en/pressroom/2026-releases/05-28-air-cargo-demand-up-april-middle-east-disruption/

**Shippers and forwarders**

Shippers are temporarily accepting surcharges that come with extending existing capacity contracts, because they are not ready to make a longer-term commitment until there are clear signs the market is normalising, per Xeneta's Chief Airfreight Officer. *Source: Xeneta / Stat Times, "Global air cargo spot rates surge 41% in May amid tensions," 6 June 2026. https://www.stattimes.com/air-cargo/global-air-cargo-spot-rates-surge-41-in-may-amid-tensions-1359396

*Analytical inference:* Forwarders currently holding block-space agreements or contracted capacity on non-Gulf corridors (Asia-Europe, transpacific) hold stronger leverage over spot-dependent shippers than at any point since 2021–2022.

Contact us Elevating Safety Standards in Air Transport Air travel demands the highest safety standards, especially when it comes to the transportation of hazardous materials. Certain items pose risks to aircraft, crew, and passengers and must be handled with strict precautions or are forbidden from air transport. This is where IATA steps in, leading the charge to ensure the highest safety levels in the air transport of dangerous goods. Through comprehensive technical expertise, industry-leading products, and customized training programs, IATA sets the stage for the safe and efficient handling of hazardous materials. The promotion and consistent implementation of these standards have raised the bar for safety in the air transport industry. Updates Need Help? Contact us Power Banks Carried by Passengers or Crew On 27 March 2026, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) introduced an addendum to the Technical Instructions regarding power banks. IATA has developed a guidance document to assist operators in assessing, managing, and implementing the changes imposed by the addendum. > View the guidance for operators (pdf) State/Operator Variations Updates State/Operator Variation ID France (FRG) FRG-07 Japan Airlines (JL) JL-11 DHL, Air Austria GmbH-DHL (Q7) Q7-06 European Air Transport Leipzig GmbH-DHL (QY) QY-06 > View full regulatory text (pdf) Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR) IATA works closely with local governments and ICAO in the development of regulations. This way, we ensure that the rules and guidelines on dangerous goods transport are effective and operational practical. The IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR) manual is the global reference for shipping dangerous goods by air and the only standard recognized by airlines. It ensures that all stakeholders, from shippers and freight forwarders to carriers, operate on a common platform of safety, reliability, and compliance. > Learn more about the IATA Dangerous Goods manuals 2026 Updates: Find out what's next in Dangerous Goods Regulations The 67th Edition of the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations brought essential updates that took effect on 1 January 2026. Stay ahead of compliance requirements. Learn more about 2026 updates Download the significant changes to the 67th Edition: English (pdf), French (pdf), German (pdf), Russian (pdf), Spanish (pdf), and Chinese (pdf) Addendum 1 to the 67th Edition in English (pdf), French (pdf), German (pdf), Russian (pdf), Spanish (pdf), Chinese (pdf) and Japanese (pdf) Training The former Appendix H in the Dangerous Goods Regulations is now a stand-alone “Dangerous Goods Training Guidance” (Edition 1). This guidance document is the practical guide for the industry players to develop their training framework in accordance with the current provisions on competency-based training and assessment (CBTA). Download the Dangerous Goods Training Guidance – EN (pdf) Also available in French (pdf), German (pdf), Spanish (pdf), and Russian (pdf) Dangerous Goods Community The IATA DG Community is the meeting place where shippers, freight forwarders, and airlines have a say. Join us to find out what information you need to know, give us feedback and share with your peers. Learn more More on Dangerous Goods DG Documentation Dangerous Goods Guidance for Passengers Batteries Shipper's Declaration Frequently Asked Questions on Transportation of Dangerous Goods by Air Classification What are dangerous goods? Dangerous Goods are items that may endanger the safety of an aircraft or persons on board the aircraft. Dangerous Goods are also known as restricted articles, hazardous materials and dangerous cargo. Many common items found in your household can be considered dangerous goods for the purpose of air transport. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) or the local Civil Aviation Authority Regulations govern their carriage onboard aircraft. How do I know if my product is a dangerous good? The Regulations place the responsibility for correct classification of dangerous goods on the shipper. The classification criteria for each class and division of dangerous goods are stipulated in DGR Section 3. Advice on the correct classification of a substance should be sought from the manufacturer or distributor of the substance. In addition, classification may be performed by an accredited testing laboratory or advice can be sought from the competent authority. I have a shipment of electronic equipment containing lithium batteries, is it classified as a dangerous good? Yes, but it may be exempted from the need of formal declaration. Check Section II of the applicable packing instruction in the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations, or our lithium battery guidance document . How do I know if my lithium batteries meet the requirements of the “UN Manual of Tests and Criteria, Part III, subsection 38.3”? Check with the manufacturer or distributor for recent production information. Battery manufacturers and distributors may have such information on their corporate websites, or through their technical support lines. It is important to note that Material Safety Data Sheets are not required in transport and not required at all for articles. This information could therefore be presented in Product Data Sheets, directly on the website, or other formats. The safety data sheet (SDS) that I have from the manufacturer really does not help to determine the correct classification and proper shipping name. What can I do? Unfortunately many SDS do not provide accurate classification for transport purposes. You should further inquire with the manufacturer or distributor or have the product tested by an authorized laboratory. Operations What's the relationship between the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations and the ICAO Technical Instructions? The IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations is a "field manual" version of the ICAO Technical Instructions . Written and edited by airline dangerous goods experts, the Dangerous Goods Regulations present the requirements for shipping dangerous goods by air in a user friendly, easy to interpret format. The DGR also includes additional information which can assist shippers in making sure their consignments are in compliance and will be accepted quickly and easily by the airlines. As IATA airlines are somewhat stricter in their requirements than the ICAO Technical Instructions, the DGR specifies more precisely how to prepare a shipment. We have done everything correct but the airline has refused to carry our shipment. What can we do? Talk to the airline and try to get as much information as possible. Check the State and operator variations of Section 2 of the IATA DGR: Have you observed all variations? Is there any likelihood the shipment may have been damaged on its way to the airport? Bear in mind that Paragraph 1.2.4 of the IATA DGR clearly stipulates that airlines are not obliged to transport a particular substance or product. They are free to impose requirements beyond and above the regulations. What is a "full" address? While there is no definition of a "full address" in the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations, we recommend that a full address be an address indicating a physical location that would be acceptable in the post (mail) in that country. This means that abbreviations would be completely acceptable. Examples of these abbreviations could be USA, UAE, AUS or TX, QC, NSW. Packaging Where can I get UN specification packaging? Appendix F in the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations contains a list of companies around the world that can supply the packaging you require. Can I use any fiberboard box to meet the limited quantity provisions? No. It is a myth that just any cardboard box will do to meet the requirements. Under the Limited Quantity provisions the fiberboard box must meet certain specifications and be capable of specified drop and stacking tests. Limited Quantity packaging is combination packaging, with inner packaging inside an outer package. The inners and outers must be constructed according to the same criteria as UN specification packaging. The inners must meet the construction criteria of DGR 6.1 and the outer the construction criteria of 6.2. So if you have glass inners - DGR 6.1.1 applies, and if you have a fiberboard outer DGR 6.2.10 applies. Almost all the General Packaging Requirements of DGR 5.0.2 and 5.0.3 for shipping dangerous goods by air apply. DGR 5.0.3.1 explains which requirements do not apply. The main difference between the UN specification package and the Limited Quantity one is the testing. The Limited Quantity packaging, when packed as for transport must be capable of withstanding a 1.2 meter drop test in a position most likely to cause most damage, without leakage, and be capable of withstanding, without breakage or leakage a 24 hour stacking test. Moyen-Orient (pdf) La industria del transporte aéreo de carga aumenta un 4,0% en abril, a pesar de las tensiones en Oriente Medio (pdf) 国际航协：中东局势动荡  4月航空货运需求增长4.0% (pdf) Demanda por Carga Aérea Sobe 4,0% em Abril apesar das interrupções no Oriente Médio (pdf) Geneva – The International Air Transport Association (IATA) released data for April 2026 global air cargo markets showing: Total demand, measured in cargo tonne-kilometers (CTK), increased by 4.0% compared to April 2025 levels (+4.0% for international operations). Capacity, measured in available cargo tonne-kilometers (ACTK), decreased by -0.4% compared to April 2025 (-0.9% for international operations). “Air cargo demand grew 4% year-on-year in April, driven by strong Asia-linked trade flows. But this positive news masks a more complex operating environment. Severe disruption at major Gulf hubs due to the war in the Middle East continued to reshape trade routes and constrain capacity on key corridors. With dedicated freighters carrying much of the growth, air cargo is once again keeping supply chains moving amid trade disruptions. The coming months will test how well the sector can absorb continued geopolitical uncertainty and elevated operating costs,” said Willie Walsh, IATA’s Director General. Several factors in the operating environment should be noted: Global trade contracted in March by 2.1% month-on-month after four consecutive months of growth, highlighting the continued vulnerability of trade momentum to geopolitical shocks. Jet fuel prices rose sharply in April, up 121.1% year-on-year, alongside a 77.7% increase in crude oil prices. Global manufacturing sentiment remained in growth territory in April, strengthening from March. The Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) rose 1.9 points to 53.4, while the PMI for new export orders reached 50.2. With both indicators above the 50-point expansion threshold, conditions remain supportive for air cargo demand. Capacity, measured in available cargo tonne-kilometers (ACTK), decreased by 4.7% compared to March 2025 (-6.8% for international operations). “Air cargo demand fell 4.8% in March compared to the previous year. This was mostly due to severe disruptions at major Gulf hubs due to war in the Middle East. The timing of the usual post–Lunar New Year slowdown also added to the decline. The underlying demand trends, at this point, appear strong and the recent World Trade Organization and International Monetary Fund revisions to trade and GDP projections continue to see growth in 2026. Importantly, air cargo networks are providing the flexibility needed to support global supply chains as they adjust to geopolitical, tariff, and operational strains. All eyes are on fuel supply and price, which are expected to test the industry’s resilience in the coming months,” said Willie Walsh, IATA’s Director General. Several factors in the operating environment should be noted: Global industrial production grew by 3.1% year-on-year in February, marking the 38th consecutive month of expansion. The global goods trade rose by 8.0% year-on-year in February. Jet fuel prices rose sharply in March, up 106.6% year-on-year, alongside a 43.1% increase in crude oil prices and a 320% surge in refining margins. Global manufacturing sentiment remained in growth territory in March, easing slightly from February. The Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) stood at 51.4. The PMI for new export orders was 50.1—both above the 50-point expansion threshold—signaling positive conditions for air cargo demand. Global air cargo spot rates surge 41% in May amid tensions Despite the sharp increase in rates, Xeneta believes pricing pressures on shippers may begin to ease in June as capacity returns and demand growth moderates. By STAT Times Loading... | 6 June 2026 7:04 AM X Global air cargo spot rates rose 41% year-on-year in May to an average of $3.40 per kg, driven by resilient demand, constrained capacity and ongoing geopolitical disruptions, according to Xeneta. The market update, released in June, showed that global air cargo demand increased 4% year-on-year while capacity recovered to 1% above last year's level. The dynamic load factor also climbed two percentage points to 61%, reflecting stronger capacity utilisation across the industry. Despite the sharp increase in rates, Xeneta believes pricing pressures on shippers may begin to ease in June as capacity returns and demand growth moderates. Niall van de Wouw, Chief Airfreight Officer at Xeneta, said: “A lot of the air cargo market statements we made in April hold true. Shippers clearly have a sense of ‘here we go again’ in terms of rate volatility, but they are adjusting and buying time by temporarily accepting the surcharges that come with extending existing capacity contracts. This is because they’re not ready to make a longer-term commitment until there are clear signs the market is normalising." Also Read - GEODIS adopts Rotate data to strengthen global air cargo insight Van de Wouw noted that some shippers are delaying long-term commitments in anticipation of lower rates. He pointed to growing frontloading activity in the ocean freight sector, where companies are accelerating production and shipments to avoid potential future cost increases and peak season surcharges. He warned that similar behaviour could eventually influence patterns of air freight demand. “On the ocean side, we see some frontloading. In many cases, the shippers doing this are acting now because they expect energy to become more costly, so they are producing now in anticipation of higher costs later, as well as to avoid traditional peak season surges in rates. But they then must move and sell their goods, and this is at a time of higher transportation costs. So, what happens? Demand rises and rates go up. It’s self-inflicted on the ocean side, but the longer the current market operating conditions continue, the more we could see this seep over into the airfreight,” van de Wouw said. Also Read - Air cargo revenues to hit $162 billion despite flat volumes At the same time, the recovery of Middle Eastern carrier capacity is expected to exert downward pressure on air freight rates in the coming weeks. Van de Wouw said: “We are on record saying rates wouldn’t come down as fast as they went up, and that is the case. It takes a while for rates to adjust to the market situation, but I would not be surprised to see year-on-year spot rate comparisons decline in June, especially as there are not a lot of industry verticals that are booming at the moment.” Although global spot rates remained elevated in May, Xeneta observed early signs of market softening. Long-term contract rates, which increased 22% year-on-year, eased after reaching a peak at the end of April, suggesting the market may have already passed its pricing high point. Further moderation is expected during the northern hemisphere summer period, when additional passenger aircraft capacity typically returns to the market. Also Read - Air India flies 1,000 tonnes of mangoes during export season The report highlighted that elevated pricing remains concentrated in specific trade corridors rather than being spread evenly across the global market. Artificial intelligence-related shipments, particularly semiconductors and data centre equipment, continued to drive strong transpacific demand. Meanwhile, renewed missile activity during the US-Iran ceasefire slowed capacity recovery into the Middle East, keeping rates on routes from Europe, South Asia and Southeast Asia to the region significantly above pre-conflict levels. Some spot rates were up by as much as 113% compared with late February. In contrast, the Europe-North America corridor experienced downward pressure on rates despite firmer demand, as expanded summer passenger schedules added substantial capacity to the transatlantic market. Also Read - Kuehne+Nagel expands Inspire air freight service Xeneta also reported continued weakness in China's low-value and e-commerce exports, which fell 11% year-on-year in April, marking a fifth consecutive monthly decline. Shipments to the United States dropped 33%, while exports to Europe and Asia Pacific recorded smaller declines. The company noted that some apparent declines may reflect a shift from individual parcel shipments to consolidated bulk air freight movements. The outlook for e-commerce faces further uncertainty as the European Union prepares to remove its €150 de minimis exemption from 1 July, replacing it with a €3 duty per imported item and an additional €2 handling fee expected later in the year. Xeneta expects the sector to adapt to the new rules rather than experience a major collapse in volumes. Trade policy developments are also drawing attention from air freight stakeholders. Following the US Supreme Court's decision to strike down the Administration's emergency IEEPA tariffs earlier this year, the US Trade Representative has proposed additional tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including the EU and China, under a separate legal framework. The proposal remains under review ahead of hearings scheduled for July. Summing up the market outlook, van de Wouw said: “Don’t expect a hot summer for air freight demand.” Tags: air cargo rates Xeneta air freight demand global logistics cargo capacity e-commerce shipments transpacific air cargo freight market outlook STAT Times One Stop destination for your Logistics & Transportation News The STAT Trade Times is now on WhatsApp Channels 🌐📱! The data, released for week 21 covering 18 to 24 May, indicates that worldwide tonnages remained flat compared to the previous week, while being approximately 2% higher than the same week in the prior year. Read also: Air Cargo Market Adjusts Amid Peak Season and Regulatory Shifts Demand for air cargo remains relatively strong, driven by supply chain lead times in the US and Europe reaching their highest levels in several months due to war-related shipping disruptions and stockpiling. Tonnages from the Asia Pacific region in week 21 were significantly higher than their levels from the same period last year, recording a 5% increase. Related Content: What Warehouses Gain when they Automate Truck Loading Despite ongoing disruptions to air cargo capacity to and from the Gulf, chargeable weight from the Middle East & South Asia (MESA) region rose by 2% week on week, though it remained slightly down by 1% year on year. On pricing, average full market air cargo rates were flat in week 21 at $3.23 per kilo, but compared to the same period last year, restricted capacity, high jet fuel costs, and greater use of freighter aircraft drove a rate increase of 35%. Average worldwide spot rates edged up by a further 1% week on week to $3.75 per kilo, driven by increases from Africa (up 4% week on week) and Asia Pacific (up 2% week on week to $5.16 per kilo). These figures are based on more than 500,000 weekly transactions covered by WorldACD’s data, resulting in average worldwide spot rates being 50% higher year on year. Spot rates from MESA rose 59% year on year to $4.26 per kilo, while spot rates from most other regions increased by more than 40% year on year, with the exception of Central & South America, which saw an 18% rise. Worldwide air cargo capacity increased by approximately 1% week on week in week 21, with freighter capacity remaining stable while passenger capacity recovered further by 2% week on week. Capacity to and from MESA experienced the largest week-on-week increase of any major global region, regaining a further 5%. However, compared to pre-war levels in week 7, capacity is down by nearly one third (32%), largely due to reductions for the Gulf, where capacity is barely half its pre-war levels (48%). These figures underscore the challenge of further scaling up air cargo capacity in the Gulf amid the current unstable context, despite carriers based outside the region increasing their freighter capacity. Compared with the same week last year, global air cargo capacity in week 21 this year was approximately 3% higher. This year-on-year growth may appear surprising given the continuing deficit in capacity flown by Gulf carriers and from the Gulf region as a whole. However, the current year-on-year increase of 3% is less than half of its level from the opening two months of 2026, prior to the war by the United States and Israel against Iran. Update: June 2, 2026 Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continued to rise over the weekend, with another round of military exchanges between U.S. and Iranian forces. U.S. forces struck Iranian radar and drone control sites on Goruk and Qeshm Island after a U.S. drone was shot down over international waters. Iran's IRGC responded by firing ballistic missiles at U.S. forces in Kuwait, where no American personnel were harmed. Iran's IRGC also claimed responsibility for the June 1 strike on Mediterranean Shipping Company's (MSC) Sariska V container ship in the port of Um-Qasr, Iraq. MSC said all crew were safe and characterized the strike as an unprovoked attack on a neutral commercial carrier with no U.S. or Israeli affiliation. The strikes came as peace talks stalled. Trump convened his national security team Friday, May 29 to make a "final determination" on a ceasefire framework, but the meeting ended without a decision. The U.S. has insisted any deal must include the reopening of the Strait, Iran renouncing nuclear weapons development, and the removal of its enriched uranium stockpile. Iran has repeatedly rejected those terms. By Monday, June 1, Iran's state-affiliated outlet Tasnim reported that Tehran was halting negotiations entirely and had resolved to fully close the Strait of Hormuz and “activate other fronts including the Bab al-Mandeb Strait,” a critical shipping lane linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Oil prices jumped more than 7% following Tasnim’s report. Update: May 27, 2026 Overnight Monday, May 25 into Tuesday, May 26 U.S. forces conducted strikes on Iranian boats that it said were attempting to lay mines, and on missile launch sites near Bandar Abbas, a southern Iranian port city on the Strait of Hormuz. Iran called it a ceasefire violation and threatened retaliation. Despite the exchange, Iran's top negotiator remained in Qatar for negotiations. Shipping remains severely disrupted: It’s reported that only three large commercial vessels transited the Strait overnight (May 25-26), all with AIS tracking switched off, while three IRGC speedboats patrolled nearby. A tanker also reported an external explosion approximately 60 nautical miles east of Muscat in the Gulf of Oman; crew was safe but bunker fuel was discharged into the sea. The U.S. Navy is escorting a small number of vessels through the Strait, including a Greek supertanker carrying two million barrels of crude to India; the vessel had been stranded since early March. Even if Iran and the U.S. negotiate an end to hostilities, analysts warn it could take months for normal traffic to resume in the Strait. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the Strait will open "one way or another" and must be toll-free, a position a senior Iranian lawmaker involved in negotiations pushed back against. Update: May 5, 2026 Yesterday, the U.S. military stated that two U.S.-flagged vessels had successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz. This transit does not indicate a general reopening of the Strait, and its practical impact on the market appears limited. At this stage, the release of additional capacity is less impactful than the sustained rise in fuel costs, which is proving increasingly difficult for carriers to absorb—particularly for smaller, less fuel-efficient vessels that are being deployed on major East-West trade lanes, where most of the largest ships are deployed. Update: May 4, 2026 Flights bound for Dubai and Sharjah are being held or diverted, following a drone attack on a key oil industrial zone in Fujairah that has disrupted UAE air space. Reports indicate that air defense operations in the area remain active. Update: April 23, 2026 At least two commercial vessels were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz yesterday. The UKMTO reported that an Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) gunboat opened fire on a container ship approximately 15 nautical miles northeast of Oman, causing significant damage to the ship’s bridge. All crew members were reported safe. Three hours later, the UKMTO reported a second incident in the Strait of Hormuz. A cargo ship located roughly 8 nautical miles off the Iranian coast indicated that it had been fired upon and came to a stop in the water. The crew was unharmed. Flexport Atlas showed two container vessels stationary near the Strait as of yesterday morning: the Panama-flagged MSC Francesca, and the Greek-operated Epaminondas. These vessels had previously broadcasted positions within the Persian Gulf. The IRGC confirmed it had intercepted both vessels and escorted them to the Iranian coast, stating that the vessels had entered the area without authorization and had disabled their Automatic Identification Systems (AIS). Following these attacks, multiple vessels that had been approaching the Strait from within the Persian Gulf reversed course. The incidents occurred one day after President Trump announced that the U.S. would extend its ceasefire with Iran, which had been set to expire on April 21. The U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in effect. Update: April 18, 2026 Less than 24 hours after Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz "completely open," the Strait is closed again. This morning, Iran's military announced that the Strait of Hormuz has reverted to "strict control," blaming the U.S. for failing to uphold its obligations under the ceasefire. Passage through the Strait now once again requires Iranian approval. The announcement came after a morning in which a minor convoy of tankers managed to exit the Persian Gulf following a brief overnight wait, which was the first meaningful commercial traffic since yesterday's opening announcement. This reversal will likely erase the market relief from yesterday, when oil prices plunged 11% following Iran's foreign minister declaring the Strait "completely open." Brent crude had fallen to approximately $89 per barrel on April 17, its lowest level since March 10, but is expected to surge again. Goldman Sachs had previously warned that another month of Hormuz closure would keep Brent above $100 throughout 2026. The U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in effect. President Trump stated yesterday that the blockade would remain until a deal is "100% complete," and warned that attacks could resume if no agreement is reached before the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire expires on April 26—now just eight days away. Impacts: Ocean: Vessels in or approaching the Strait of Hormuz should expect delays or denial of transit. Any transit windows may be short-lived and subject to sudden reversal. Air: No new direct impacts on air space, though elevated regional risk continues to affect carrier scheduling and fuel surcharges. Jet fuel prices, which had begun to ease on yesterday's oil drop, are expected to resume upward pressure. Bunker Fuel and Surcharges: Emergency bunker surcharges remain in effect across major trades. Any easing in bunker fuel costs anticipated from yesterday's crude price drop is now unlikely to materialize. Carriers are expected to maintain or increase surcharge levels. The situation remains highly fluid. We will continue to provide updates as conditions evolve. Monitor real-time vessel movements at Flexport Atlas . Update: April 17, 2026 Today, Iran re-opened the Strait of Hormuz for all commercial shipping through the remainder of the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire. The ceasefire is due to conclude on April 26, 2026. Iran clarified that all vessels must follow a “coordinated route” while transiting the Strait. Additionally, it is currently unclear whether vessels will be required to pay a toll. Brent crude oil futures dropped more than 10% today, falling to about $89 per barrel. President Trump indicated that the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Strait will remain in effect until a deal between both sides is “100% complete.” Update: April 13, 2026 This morning, the U.S. initiated a naval blockade targeting Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump stated on Truth Social that any Iranian “fast attack ships” approaching the blockade zone would be destroyed. The U.S. military indicated that the blockade applies specifically to ships traveling to or from Iranian ports and coastal waters, while other commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz to reach non-Iranian destinations would still be permitted to pass. Iran had previously indicated that it would retaliate if the U.S. proceeded with the blockade. On April 7, the U.S. and Iran agreed upon a temporary two-week ceasefire. The ceasefire appears to remain in place, despite the blockade. Impacts: Given the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in late February, the blockade does not represent a significant new disruption to ocean shipping at this time. However, Brent crude oil futures climbed 7% this morning, again exceeding $100 per barrel. Brent crude prices had eased following last week’s ceasefire announcement, but ongoing relief in bunker costs—and hence the previously anticipated relief in carrier emergency bunker charges—now appears to be less realistic. Global air cargo tonnage, pricing and capacity decline in early May Traffic from Asia Pacific and MESA weakened after holiday-driven demand eased, while annual volumes and spot rates remained above last year. By - STAT Times Update: 2026-05-18 07:45 GMT Global air cargo volumes, pricing and capacity declined in the first full week of May as the holiday period in Asia ended and flower shipments linked to Mother’s Day eased, according to WorldACD Weekly Air Cargo data. Despite the week-on-week decline, both traffic and pricing remained higher on an annual basis. Global tonnage fell 3% week on week (WoW), taking the combined decline for weeks 18 and 19 to 6% compared with the previous two weeks, based on more than 500,000 weekly transactions covered by WorldACD’s data. The fall was largely driven by the end of the Mother’s Day flower surge, which reduced volumes from Central and South America (CSA) by 19% WoW and 9% over the two-week period. Chargeable weight from Asia Pacific dropped 5% WoW and 8% over two weeks following the end of the Super Golden Week holiday. Tonnage from the Middle East & South Asia (MESA) region declined 4% WoW, while traffic from North America and Europe increased 5% and 2% respectively as demand from Asia rebounded after the holiday period. On a year-on-year (YoY) basis, global tonnage rose 5%, with increases from all origin regions except Africa, which recorded an 11% decline. The Super Golden Week holiday, combining Japan’s Golden Week with public holidays in China and South Korea, reduced outbound volumes from Asia Pacific by 9% WoW to both Europe and the United States. Chargeable weight from Japan dropped 44% to the US and 54% to Europe. While volumes from Asia Pacific to the US declined across all sectors, chargeable weight from Vietnam to Europe rose 22%. Exports to other European destinations fell, except from Thailand, which remained flat, and Taiwan, which increased 1%. Volumes from MESA dropped 5% WoW to both the US and Europe, although trends varied across markets. Traffic to Europe declined due to double-digit falls from Dubai and Bangladesh, while chargeable weight to the US from Dubai increased 65% after a double-digit decline the previous week. However, volumes from India and Sri Lanka to the US declined 7% and 5% respectively. On an annual basis, chargeable weight from MESA increased 11% to the US but declined 1% to Europe, resulting in overall growth of 6% for MESA-origin airfreight. Chargeable weight from Asia Pacific to Europe slipped 1% YoY due to lower tonnage from Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong, while exports to the US increased 33%, supported by growth across most origins except Indonesia, down 21%, and Japan, down 2%. Volumes from China and Hong Kong to the US increased by nearly 50%. Global air cargo pricing also declined as demand slowed. Average rates fell 3% WoW to $3.22, matching the decline in chargeable weight. With the exception of Europe, where rates rose 1%, and North America, where pricing remained flat, rates declined across all regions. CSA recorded the steepest drop at 8%, followed by Africa at 7%, reflecting the end of flower shipments for Mother’s Day. On a YoY basis, CSA was the only origin region to record single-digit pricing growth at 7%, while other regions reported increases ranging from 22% in North America to 56% in MESA. Overall pricing increased 39% YoY, while spot prices were 51% higher. Spot rates from MESA to Europe declined 3% WoW, with low single-digit falls across most origins except Dubai, which rose 7%. Pricing to the US also declined 3% WoW due to single-digit drops across MESA origins. On an annual basis, spot rates from MESA to the US increased 60%, led by a 135% rise from Dubai. Dubai also recorded a 181% increase in spot rates to Europe, contributing to a 72% rise for MESA overall. Global air cargo capacity declined 2% WoW following flat growth in week 18 as the flower rush and Super Golden Week ended. Capacity dropped 4% in CSA, 3% in Asia Pacific, and 2% in both North America and Africa. Europe and MESA remained flat, indicating slower momentum in rebuilding capacity in the latter region. Freighter operations by Gulf-based carriers have largely recovered, although passenger services are not expected to fully return until conflict conditions stabilise and traveller confidence improves. Rising fuel costs have also led airlines to reduce or cancel unprofitable routes, particularly regional services operated by narrowbody aircraft, although the impact on cargo capacity has remained limited. Airlines cut 13,000 flights in May, and industry observers expect further schedule changes as aviation fuel prices are unlikely to decline significantly in the near term. sections.md:
The regulatory timeline is published and sourced. FACT: The IMO has set the following milestone sequence: "October 2025 (MEPC/ES.2): Adoption of the amendments during an extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee. Spring 2026 (MEPC 84): Approval of detailed implementation guidelines. 2027: Expected entry into force, 16 months after adoption (in accordance with MARPOL articles)." *Source: IMO Press Briefing, IMO, 11 April 2025. https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx

MONITORING — MEPC 84 Implementation Guidelines: The Spring 2026 MEPC 84 session is the next conversion trigger. *Analytical inference:* The implementation guidelines approved at MEPC 84 will set the operational detail that determines how Greenhouse Gas Fuel Intensity (GFI) thresholds are calculated, how remedial units are priced, and how the IMO Net-Zero Fund contribution mechanism works in practice. Until those guidelines are published, cost-per-tonne estimates and compliance cost projections remain indicative. Re-check window: Q3 2026 (following MEPC 84 outcomes).

The DNV classification rules cycle has its own conversion trigger. FACT: The 77 documents in DNV's 2026 hearing are "planned for publication on 1 July 2026." *Source: DNV News, "DNV rules 2026 – Hearing period now open," DNV, 2 March 2026. https://www.dnv.com/news/2026/dnv-rules-2026-hearing-period-now-open/

*Analytical inference:* Publication on 1 July 2026 means vessel owners and charterers will have approximately 18 months between final DNV rule publication and the 2027 IMO entry-into-force date to apply for relevant notations (Shore Power Ready, ULEV, Battery Ready) and initiate any required surveys. For workspaces chartering or booking ocean capacity on long-term contracts, the July 2026 DNV publication date is the practical start of carrier differentiation on these metrics.

**Alternative fuel fleet growth is accelerating toward a structural market shift.** FACT: "From January to April 2025, the share of alternative-fuel newbuild orders rose further to 63%." FACT: "By 2024, vessels powered by marine clean alternative fuels accounted for 43.2% of the global fleet by deadweight tonnage, marking a two-percentage-point increase from 2023." *Source: Frontiers in Marine Science, Frontiers/Shasha Wang et al., 12 December 2025. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1683017/full

*Analytical inference:* When over 60% of newbuild orders are alternative-fuel vessels, the conventional-fuel fleet becomes a progressively smaller share of capacity being added. For workspaces that place volume on spot or short-term ocean contracts, access to compliant capacity in 2027–2030 is a booking-desk problem, not only a compliance problem.

---

**IMO member states** are the binding authority. FACT: "MARPOL Annex VI currently has 108 Parties, covering 97% of the world's merchant shipping fleet by tonnage." *Source: IMO Press Briefing, IMO, 11 April 2025. https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx

*Analytical inference:* With 108 parties covering 97% of tonnage, the jurisdictional reach is effectively universal for ocean freight. Flag-state shopping to avoid the framework is structurally closed off at current MARPOL participation levels.

**National blocs are competing on fuel standard-setting, not on whether to decarbonize.** FACT: The Frontiers research identifies that "China's '1+N' policy system emphasizes top-down coordination, the EU relies on carbon trading mechanisms and mandatory measures like FuelEU Maritime, Japan prioritizes safety standards (e.g., ClassNK guidelines), and Singapore adopts pragmatic policies to establish a green fuel hub." *Source: Frontiers in Marine Science, Frontiers/Shasha Wang et al., 12 December 2025. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1683017/full

*Analytical inference:* The competitive dynamic is not deregulation vs. regulation — it is standard-setting influence. Singapore's stated ambition to become a green fuel hub, the EU's FuelEU Maritime, and Japan's ClassNK safety-led approach are all positioning plays for where fuel supply chains, bunkering infrastructure, and compliance verification services locate. For workspaces routing ocean cargo through Singapore, Rotterdam, or Tokyo, the bunkering cost and availability picture will diverge by port in 2026–2028.

**DNV** is positioning its classification tools to track the regulatory curve. *Analytical inference:* The 2026 rules hearing — which introduces Shore Power Ready, Battery Ready, ULEV qualifiers, and an extended fuel tank survey programme — reflects DNV anticipating that fleet owners will need classification evidence of readiness ahead of the 2027 entry-into-force date. This is a competitive positioning move by a classification society, not a neutral technical update.

**Low-emission shipping nations and the IMO Net-Zero Fund** are the designed beneficiaries of the pricing mechanism. FACT: Revenues from the IMO Net-Zero Fund "will then be disbursed to: Reward low-emission ships; Support innovation, research, infrastructure and just transition initiatives in developing countries; Fund training, technology transfer and capacity building to support the IMO GHG Strategy; and Mitigate negative impacts on vulnerable States, such as Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries." *Source: IMO Press Briefing, IMO, 11 April 2025. https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx

---

**The IMO Net-Zero Framework has cleared its most critical regulatory hurdle and is now on a fixed entry-into-force trajectory.** FACT: "The 83rd MEPC session, held in London on 7–11 April 2025, approved draft amendments to Annex VI of the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), marking the world's first regulatory framework combining mandatory emission limits with greenhouse gas pricing in the shipping industry." *Source: Frontiers in Marine Science, "Global coordination and challenges of technical standards and application specifications for marine clean alternative fuels," Frontiers/Shasha Wang et al., 12 December 2025. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1683017/full

FACT: The IMO press briefing confirms the framework "will be included in a new Chapter 5 of Annex VI (Prevention of air pollution from ships) to the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL)," combining "a new fuel standard for ships and a global pricing mechanism for emissions," and was "set to be formally adopted in October 2025 before entry into force in 2027." *Source: IMO Press Briefing, "IMO approves net-zero regulations for global shipping," IMO, 11 April 2025. https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx

FACT: The framework targets "large ocean-going ships over 5,000 gross tonnage, which emit 85% of the total CO₂ emissions from international shipping." *Source: IMO Press Briefing, IMO, 11 April 2025. https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx

A parallel signal is moving in DNV's classification rules cycle. FACT: "DNV has submitted its class rules and standards for industry hearing, open for comments from 1 March to 12 April [2026]. This year's hearing covers 77 documents, planned for publication on 1 July 2026." *Source: DNV News, "DNV rules 2026 – Hearing period now open," DNV, 2 March 2026. https://www.dnv.com/news/2026/dnv-rules-2026-hearing-period-now-open/

Within that rules cycle, DNV has proposed a directly emissions-relevant notation: FACT: "New qualifier ULEV for class notation ER, emission reductions system for NOx or SOx to signify an ultra low emission vessel." *Source: DNV News, "DNV rules 2026 – Hearing period now open," DNV, 2 March 2026. https://www.dnv.com/news/2026/dnv-rules-2026-hearing-period-now-open/

*Operational implication:* These two signals are coupled. The IMO framework creates the regulatory demand; the DNV classification cycle creates the operational tooling — vessel notations, survey programmes, and shore-power readiness qualifiers — that carriers will use to demonstrate compliance. Both signals are live simultaneously in Q2 2026.

---

**COMPETITIVE EDGE — workspaces that embed GFI-aware contract language and carrier selection criteria now, before the 2027 entry-into-force, have a concrete lead over peers who treat this as a post-2026 problem.**

*Analytical inference:* The framework creates a two-tier carrier market: vessels with surplus units (low-GFI, alternative-fuel) that can offer clean-cargo credentials, and vessels with deficit units (high-GFI, conventional fuel) that will carry surcharge exposure. Workspaces that identify which carriers their ocean volumes currently flow through, and whether those carriers are positioned on the surplus or deficit side, can make informed routing adjustments before rates diverge visibly.

*Specific carrier-level GFI positioning data not available from primary sources as of 2026-06-03.* DNV's Veracity data platform and Clarksons Research are candidate sources for fleet-level fuel efficiency data, but specific carrier rankings require subscription access not reflected in the provided source content.

**Alternative fuel fleet ordering concentration creates an access dynamic.** FACT: "In the first quarter of 2022, alternative-fuel vessels accounted for 61% of total newbuild orders by gross tonnage. In terms of fuel types, LNG remains the mainstream alternative, representing 94% of orders by vessel count." *Source: Frontiers in Marine Science, Frontiers/Shasha Wang et al., 12 December 2025. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1683017/full

*Analytical inference:* LNG-dominant newbuild ordering means the near-term alternative-fuel fleet is predominantly LNG-powered, not ammonia or hydrogen. LNG has lower lifecycle GHG intensity than HFO but remains a fossil fuel. Under a well-to-wake GFI calculation, LNG vessels may occupy a middle band — better than HFO, not sufficient for maximum surplus-unit eligibility. Workspaces seeking to claim the highest available green-freight credentials for client reporting should clarify with carriers which fuel type and GFI calculation methodology applies to specific voyages.

*Analytical inference:* The national standard fragmentation identified in the Frontiers research — China's top-down policy, EU's FuelEU Maritime, Japan's ClassNK safety standards, Singapore's hub strategy — means that on transpacific, Europe-Asia, and intra-Asia trade lanes, the compliance cost structure and fuel availability will differ. Workspaces with trade lanes spanning multiple of these regulatory zones face a mosaic compliance picture, not a single global rate adjustment.

**Named competitor positioning:** *Specific competitor freight forwarder positioning on IMO Net-Zero Framework not available from primary sources as of 2026-06-03.*

---

| # | Title | Issuing Body | Date | Type | URL |
|---|-------|-------------|------|------|-----|
| 1 | IMO approves net-zero regulations for global shipping | International Maritime Organization (IMO) | 11 April 2025 | Intergovernmental body position | https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx |
| 2 | Global coordination and challenges of technical standards and application specifications for marine clean alternative fuels in the IMO's new emission reduction regulations | Frontiers in Marine Science / Wang et al. | 12 December 2025 | Peer-reviewed academic research | https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1683017/full |
| 3 | DNV rules 2026 – Hearing period now open | DNV | 2 March 2026 | Industry body / classification society announcement | https://www.dnv.com/news/2026/dnv-rules-2026-hearing-period-now-open/ |

---

**Priority 1 — Map ocean carrier exposure before MEPC 84 guidelines publish (target: Q3 2026)**
*Action:* Identify the top 5 ocean carriers by volume and route. Request their published CII ratings, fuel type mix, and any stated GFI readiness position for 2027. This creates a baseline before the guidelines give carriers a formal compliance score to disclose.
*Who is affected:* Operations leads managing ocean bookings; commercial leadership quoting clients on total landed cost.
*Why now:* MEPC 84 guidelines (Spring 2026) are the trigger that converts this from a forward signal to an active pricing mechanism. Knowing carrier exposure before guidelines publish means the workspace responds to rate changes with data, not reactively.

**Priority 2 — Insert GFI / IMO Net-Zero awareness clauses into ocean freight rate negotiations in 2026**
*Action:* When renewing or negotiating ocean freight agreements for 2027 coverage, include explicit acknowledgment of the IMO Net-Zero Framework surcharge mechanism and request carrier disclosure of their GFI compliance cost pass-through methodology.
*Legal Confirmation Required:* The specific drafting of such clauses and their enforceability under the applicable contract law require counsel review.
*Why now:* Contracts agreed in 2026 without this language will have no mechanism to allocate the surcharge risk introduced in 2027.

**Priority 3 — Monitor DNV July 2026 rules publication for vessel notation signals**
*Action:* When DNV publishes its final 2026 rules on 1 July 2026, check which carriers have vessels carrying or applying for ULEV, Shore Power, and Battery Ready notations. This is the first concrete fleet-level compliance differentiation signal.
*Re-check window:* July 2026.

**Priority 4 — Prepare Scope 3 reporting infrastructure for well-to-wake data**
*Action:* The GFI calculation uses a well-to-wake approach. If the workspace's Scope 3 reporting currently uses tank-to-wake emission factors for ocean freight, the methodology gap should be identified now. Work with carriers or emissions data providers to understand whether well-to-wake voyage data will be available from 2027.
*Analytical inference:* Workspaces whose clients request ISO 14083 or GHG Protocol-aligned Scope 3 reports will face client-side pressure to shift to well-to-wake ocean freight emissions data once the IMO framework makes this the regulatory standard for vessels.

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- The IMO has approved a mandatory net-zero framework that applies to large ocean-going vessels from 2027. This is confirmed by the IMO's own press briefing from April 2025 and is not speculative.
- The framework combines a fuel intensity standard and a pricing mechanism — two levers that will affect carrier operating costs, and by extension freight rates, from 2027 onward.
- DNV's 2026 classification rules hearing introduces vessel notations (ULEV, Shore Power Ready, Battery Ready) that will become a quality and compliance differentiator for vessel selection by 2027.
- Over 43% of the global fleet by deadweight tonnage was already powered by alternative fuels as of 2024, and 63% of newbuild orders in early 2025 were alternative-fuel vessels — so fleet transition is already structurally underway, not hypothetical.

**Questions the workspace can pose to clients:**

- Which of your ocean lanes carry the highest volume, and do you know whether your current carriers are investing in alternative-fuel fleet renewal?
- Does your sustainability reporting require well-to-wake emissions data from ocean freight? If so, you will need GFI-verified voyage data from carriers from 2027 onward.
- Are any of your ocean shipments routed through ports where shore power requirements are advancing (EU ports, California)? Carrier vessel notation status will become relevant to your Scope 3 reporting.

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not quote per-tonne GFI surcharge figures — the implementation guidelines from MEPC 84 have not been published as of the date of this brief. Any cost estimate is speculative until those guidelines are finalised.
- Do not describe the framework as "in force" — entry into force is expected in 2027, 16 months after October 2025 adoption. As of Q2 2026, the framework is adopted but not yet in force.
- *Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether specific contractual surcharge pass-through clauses in existing ocean freight agreements are triggered by IMO GFI compliance costs requires legal review against the specific contract language.

---

[corridor_identity] No verbatim UN/LOCODE port-pair and mode were located together in the captured source text for this record-grade item — corridor identity is only stated when both ends are named together. A full-brief regrounding will re-examine this gap when this item upgrades from record to brief.

**COST ALERT — Ocean freight cost structure is changing at the fuel and pricing layers simultaneously.**

The IMO Net-Zero Framework imposes two cost mechanisms on carriers, each of which will pass through to freight rates:

**GFI compliance cost:** FACT: "Ships emitting above GFI thresholds will have to acquire remedial units to balance its deficit emissions, while those using zero or near-zero GHG technologies will be eligible for financial rewards." *Source: IMO Press Briefing, IMO, 11 April 2025. https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx

*Operational implication:* The remedial-unit cost is a variable per-voyage charge that carriers will seek to recover through fuel surcharges or rate adjustments. For workspaces moving ocean freight on routes served by older, less fuel-efficient tonnage, the surcharge exposure is higher than for routes where newer alternative-fuel vessels dominate capacity.

*Specific cost-per-remedial-unit figure not available from primary sources as of 2026-06-03.* The implementation guidelines expected from MEPC 84 (Spring 2026) are the authoritative source for this figure. Until published, any per-tonne cost estimate carries analytical-inference status only.

**Fuel transition cost:** FACT: The framework aims to "accelerate the introduction of zero and near zero GHG fuels, technologies and energy sources." *Source: IMO Press Briefing, IMO, 11 April 2025. https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-approves-netzero-regulations.aspx FACT: The Frontiers research identifies that "shipping companies focus primarily on the integrity of the fuel supply chain, operating costs, and safety" when selecting alternative fuels, and flags "uneven infrastructure deployment" as a major challenge. *Source: Frontiers in Marine Science, Frontiers/Shasha Wang et al., 12 December 2025. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1683017/full

*Operational implication:* Uneven bunkering infrastructure means alternative-fuel cost premiums will vary by port. Routes through Singapore (green fuel hub ambition), Rotterdam (EU FuelEU Maritime incentive zone), and major Chinese ports (top-down coordination policy) will likely have better alternative-fuel availability and more competitive pricing than secondary ports — creating a route-level cost divergence for workspaces that cannot consolidate volumes through hub ports.

**By cargo vertical, for workspaces with ocean as a secondary or tertiary mode:**

- *Analytical inference:* For workspaces moving high-value, time-sensitive cargo (live events, fine art, luxury goods, film and TV production equipment) primarily by air, ocean freight is typically a minority share of freight spend. The direct cost exposure from GFI surcharges is therefore proportionally contained. However, where ocean is used for lower-urgency high-cube or heavy shipments — set components, automotive support equipment, display materials — the surcharge layer will compound with existing ocean rate volatility.
- *Analytical inference:* For workspaces moving humanitarian cargo, the GFI pricing mechanism's Fund disbursements to developing countries and SIDS are a signal that the IMO has designed a partial offset mechanism for vulnerable routes. Whether this translates to rate protection on specific humanitarian lanes requires carrier-specific data not available in current sources.

**DNV classification rule changes — shore power and emission notation implications:**

*Operational implication:* The proposed Shore Power Ready and Shore Power (IEC / Permanent) class notations within DNV's 2026 hearing signal that shore power capability is moving from optional to classification-trackable. For workspaces whose ocean carriers call at ports where shore power mandates are active or advancing (EU ports under FuelEU Maritime, California ports under existing regulation), the notation status of chartered vessels will become a contract-conversation point by 2027.

---

Diversity, equity & inclusion Life @ DNV Media Newsroom Statistics and Insights Events Podcast: Trust and transformations Blogs: Energy in transition Contact us Sign in to Veracity Global MAIN WEBSITES China Germany Italy Netherlands Norway Spain United Kingdom USA LOCAL WEBSITES: Africa (French) Africa (English) Argentina Australia and NZ Belgium Brazil Canada Chile Croatia Czech Republic Denmark Finland France Hungary India Japan Korea Malaysia Mexico Middle East Poland Singapore Slovakia Sweden Taiwan Open search News from DNV 2026 DNV rules 2026 – Hearing period now open DNV rules 2026 – Hearing period now open DNV has submitted its class rules and standards for industry hearing, open for comments from 1 March to 12 April. This year’s hearing covers 77 documents, planned for publication on 1 July 2026. This update highlights the key proposed changes and explains how to submit feedback. SHARE: Information for: Ship owners, managers, yards, manufacturers, flag states, suppliers and design offices. NEED TO KNOW   The hearing period is open from 1 March to 12 April 77 documents — overview of the changes follows below Comments on the rules and standard changes to be provided in DNV’s Rules and Standards Explorer DNV welcomes comments from all interested parties. Feedback on rule proposals is part of a thorough quality assurance process for DNV’s rules and standards. The complete list of documents submitted for hearing can be found in the Documents on hearing tab in the Rules and Standards Explorer . DNV ship rules (DNV-RU-SHIP):   Liquified gas tankers: new qualifiers visualizing vessels cargo capabilities and introduced new qualifier FSU for gas carriers used for storage and delivery of LNG to shore (Pt.5 Ch.7). Class notation Fish carrier is restructured to cover transport of fish in general and making stability requirements mandatory for transport of live fish only (Pt.5 Ch.10 Sec.18). Fishing vessels: adapting to industry standard and current statutory codes (Pt.5 Ch.12). New qualifier Ready for class notation Battery to signify a vessel being prepared for later battery installations (Pt.6 Ch.2 Sec.1). New qualifier T for class notation Strengthened signifying that T-bars provided on the cargo deck for securing wooden sheeting, are strengthened to support temporary equipment and securing cargo (Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.2.)  New class notation FL for extended fatigue life (Pt.6 Ch.1 Sec.17). New qualifier P PV for class notation VCS , vapour control systems, for cargo tanks designed to withstand higher pressure and thus to reduce VOC emissions (Pt.6 Ch.4 Sec.11). For class notation Shore power : new qualifier IEC for meeting complete IEC requirements, new qualifier Permanent for vessels utilizing shore power continuously and introducing new class notation Shore power ready to signify a vessel being prepared for later shore power installations (Pt.6 Ch.7 Sec.5). New qualifier ULEV for class notation ER , emission reductions system for NO x or SO x to signify an ultra low emission vessel (Pt.6 Ch.7 Sec.7). Alternative survey programme: new qualifier Fuel for class notation ASP enabling an extended and flexible scheduling of internal gas fuel tank(s) survey (Pt.6 Ch.9 Sec.8). Offshore rules (DNV-RU-OU): New class notation FL for design fatigue life with qualifiers specifying the fatigue life in years and the expiry year for the design life (DNV-RU-OU-0101, 0102, 0103 and 0104). Updated the advanced fatigue life notation FMS , new qualifiers specifying the selected design fatigue factor (DFF) level, fatigue life in years and expiry year (DNV-RU-OU-0101, 0102, 0103 and 0104). New class notation NUI for normally unattended installations (DNV-RU-OU-0102, 0103). Added class notation CMON for construction monitoring for fatigue critical details (DNV-RU-OU-0101, 0102, 0103 and 0104). Class retention requirements added for class notation Sustainability (DNV-RU-OU-0300). New requirements for floating fish farm structures that are made of composites or polymers (DNV-RU-OU-0503). Complete rewriting of in-service class requirements for floating offshore wind farms, enabling alternative ways of survey and follow-up (DNV-RU-OU-0512). Offshore standards (DNV-OS): Restructured DNV‑OS‑A101 to clearly distinguish common requirements that apply to all units from the additional requirements that apply to specific unit types, such as production, drilling, and well intervention units (DNV-OS-A101). Added requirements for NUI notation, where the risk to personnel is normally reduced and this can be reflected in the system design (DNV-OS-A101). Updated the requirements for FMS notation, including an option to select between two design fatigue factors (DNV-OS-C101). Removed requirements for towing equipment, class requirement now only cover the towing fittings (DNV-OS-C101, DNV-OS-C102). Updated requirements for support of heavy equipment and topside foundations, including winches (DNV-OS-C102). Recommendations All stakeholders are encouraged to review the proposals relevant to them. Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships --> About IMO FAQs History of IMO Careers at IMO Procurement Membership Structure Council Candidates Strategic Plan Conventions Documents and Resources IMO Events Calendar of Events Affiliated Bodies and Programmes World Maritime University (WMU) and IMO International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) Contact Us Financial Statements Summary Media Centre Press Briefings Meeting Summaries and schedule Secretary-General What's New Hot Topics IMO News Magazine Attending IMO Meetings IMO Events Our Work Maritime Safety Maritime Security and Piracy Marine Environment Legal Affairs Human Element Facilitation Member State Audit Scheme Implementation of Instruments Support Technical Cooperation Partnerships and Projects Conferences External Relations Reducing Administrative Burdens Circulars Publications Distributors' Details Catalogue ＆ Code Listings Just Published Future Titles Flyers Supplements Copyright and Permission Requests Counterfeit copies IMDG Code The IMO Bookshelf The IMO-Vega Database Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) Listing of current IMO publications Knowledge Centre Search the MKC Online Catalogue How and Where to Find IMO Information Index of IMO Resolutions Current Awareness Bulletin Conferences and Meetings Maritime Facts and Figures Resources for Seafarers Contacts Contact us Careers English Français Español IMO WEB ACCOUNTS Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships Home Our Work Marine Environment Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships Although air pollution from ships does not have the direct cause and effect associated with, for example, an oil spill incident, it causes a cumulative effect that contributes to the overall air quality problems encountered by populations in many areas, and also affects the natural environment, such as tough acid rain. MARPOL Annex VI, first adopted in 1997, limits the main air pollutants contained in ships exhaust gas, including sulphur oxides (SO x ) and nitrous oxides (NO x ), and prohibits deliberate emissions of ozone depleting substances (ODS). MARPOL Annex VI also regulates shipboard incineration, and the emissions of volatile organic compounds (VOC) from tankers. Following entry into force of MARPOL Annex VI on 19 May 2005, the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC), at its 53rd session (July 2005), agreed to revise MARPOL Annex VI with the aim of significantly strengthening the emission limits in light of technological improvements and implementation experience. As a result of three years examination, MEPC 58 (October 2008) adopted the revised MARPOL Annex VI and the associated NO x Technical Code 2008, which entered into force on 1 July 2010. Revised MARPOL Annex VI The main changes to MARPOL Annex VI are a progressive reduction globally in emissions of SO x , NO x and particulate matter and the introduction of emission control areas (ECAs) to reduce emissions of those air pollutants further in designated sea areas. Under the revised MARPOL Annex VI, the global sulphur limit will be reduced from current 3.50% to 0.50%, effective from 1 January 2020, subject to a feasibility review to be completed no later than 2018. MEPC 70 (October 2016) considered an assessment of fuel oil availability to inform the decision to be taken by the Parties to MARPOL Annex VI, and decided that the fuel oil standard (0.50% sulphur limit) shall become effective on 1 January 2020. The limits applicable in ECAs for SO x and particulate matter were reduced to 0.10%, from 1 January 2015. Progressive reductions in NO x emissions from marine diesel engines installed on ships are also included, with a "Tier II" emission limit for engines installed on a ship constructed on or after 1 January 2011; and a more stringent "Tier III" emission limit for engines installed on a ship constructed on or after 1 January 2016 operating in ECAs (North American Emission Control Area and the U.S. Caribbean Sea Emission Control Area). Marine diesel engines installed on a ship constructed on or after 1 January 1990 but prior to 1 January 2000 are required to comply with "Tier I" emission limits, if an approved method for that engine has been certified by an Administration. The revised NO x Technical Code 2008 includes a new chapter based on the agreed approach for regulation of existing (pre-2000) engines established in MARPOL Annex VI, provisions for a direct measurement and monitoring method, a certification procedure for existing engines and test cycles to be applied to Tier II and Tier III engines. MEPC 66 (April 2014) adopted amendments to regulation 13 of MARPOL Annex VI regarding the effective date of NO x Tier III standards. The amendments provide for the Tier III NO x standards to be applied to a marine diesel engine that is installed on a ship constructed on or after 1 January 2016 and which operates in the North American Emission Control Area or the U.S. Caribbean Sea Emission Control Area that are designated for the control of NO x emissions. In addition, the Tier III requirements would apply to installed marine diesel engines when operated in other emission control areas which might be designated in the future for Tier III NO x control. Tier III would apply to ships constructed on or after the date of adoption by the Marine Environment Protection Committee of such an emission control area, or a later date as may be specified in the amendment designating the NO x Tier III emission control area. Further, the Tier III requirements do not apply to a marine diesel engine installed on a ship constructed prior to 1 January 2021 of less than 500 gross tonnage, of 24 m or over in length, which has been specifically designed and is used solely, for recreational purposes. Revisions to the regulations for ozone-depleting substances, volatile organic compounds, shipboard incineration, reception facilities and fuel oil quality were also made with regulations on fuel oil availability added. The revised measures are expected to have a significant beneficial impact on the atmospheric environment and on human health, particularly for those people living in port cities and coastal communities.
