regulations for global shipping OCENA ENVIRONMENT SHIP EMISSIONS --> Home Media Centre Latest News IMO approves net-zero regulations for global shipping Draft regulations will set mandatory marine fuel standard and GHG emissions pricing for shipping to address climate change. ​The IMO Net-zero Framework will combine mandatory emissions limits and GHG pricing across an entire industry sector.    The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has achieved another important step towards establishing a legally binding framework to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ships globally, aiming for net-zero emissions by or around, i.e close to 2050.   The IMO Net-zero Framework is the first in the world to combine mandatory emissions limits and GHG pricing across an entire industry sector.    Approved by the Marine Environment Protection Committee during its 83rd session (MEPC 83) from 7–11 April 2025, the measures include a new fuel standard for ships and a global pricing mechanism for emissions.   These measures, set to be formally adopted in October 2025 before entry into force in 2027, will become mandatory for large ocean-going ships over 5,000 gross tonnage, which emit 85% of the total CO 2 emissions from international shipping.   Closing the meeting , IMO Secretary-General Mr. Arsenio Dominguez commended the spirit of cooperation and commitment demonstrated by Member States this week. He stated:  “The approval of draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI mandating the IMO net-zero framework represents another significant step in our collective efforts to combat climate change, to modernize shipping and demonstrates that IMO delivers on its commitments.   “Now, it is important to continue working together, engaging in dialogue and listening to one another, if we are to create the conditions for successful adoption.”   Key elements of the IMO Net-Zero Framework  The IMO Net-Zero Framework will be included in a new Chapter 5 of Annex VI (Prevention of air pollution from ships) to the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships ( MARPOL ).   MARPOL Annex VI currently has 108 Parties, covering 97% of the world’s merchant shipping fleet by tonnage, and already includes mandatory energy efficiency requirements for ships.  The goal is to achieve the climate targets set out in the 2023 IMO Strategy on the Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships , accelerate the introduction of zero and near zero GHG fuels, technologies and energy sources, and support a just and equitable transition.    Under the draft regulations, ships will be required to comply with:  Global fuel standard : Ships must reduce, over time, their annual greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) – that is, how much GHG is emitted for each unit of energy used. This is calculated using a well-to-wake approach.   Global economic measure : Ships emitting above GFI thresholds will have to acquire remedial units to balance its deficit emissions, while those using zero or near-zero GHG technologies will be eligible for financial rewards.   Ensuring compliance   There will be two levels of compliance with GHG Fuel Intensity targets: a Base Target and a Direct Compliance Target at which ships would be eligible to earn “surplus units”.    Ships that emit above the set thresholds can balance their emissions deficit by:   Transferring surplus units from other ships;    Using surplus units they have already banked;    Using remedial units acquired through contributions to the IMO Net-Zero Fund.    IMO Net-Zero Fund  The IMO Net-Zero Fund will be established to collect pricing contributions from emissions. These revenues will then be disbursed to:   Reward low-emission ships;   Support innovation, research, infrastructure and just transition initiatives in developing countries;   Fund training, technology transfer and capacity building to support the IMO GHG Strategy; and   Mitigate negative impacts on vulnerable States, such as Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries.   Next steps  Upon approval, the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI will be formally circulated to IMO Member States, followed by:  October 2025 (MEPC/ES.2) : Adoption of the amendments during an extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee.   Spring 2026 (MEPC 84) : Approval of detailed implementation guidelines.   2027 : Expected entry into force, 16 months after adoption (in accordance with MARPOL articles).   Other MEPC 83 outcomes  The meeting discussed a range of issues related to protecting the marine environment from shipping activities, with the following key outcomes:  Adoption of 2025 Action Plan to combat marine plastic litter;   Progress in the review of the Ballast Water Management Convention;  Approval of a proposal to designate the North-East Atlantic as an Emission Control Area and agreement in principle to designate two new Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas off South America’s Pacific coast;  Approval of the draft Work plan on the development of a regulatory framework for the use of Onboard Carbon Capture Storage systems (OCCS)  Approval of draft amendments to regulation 27 of MARPOL Annex VI regarding accessibility of the IMO Data Collection System  Adoption of amendments to the 2021 Guidelines on the operational carbon intensity reduction factors relative to reference lines (CII reduction factors guidelines, G3)  Approval of a new output to develop a legally binding framework on biofouling management, to prevent the spread of harmful invasive aquatic species  Full meeting summary here .  Links View photo gallery  and download  b-roll Secretary-General's opening remarks / closing remarks Full text of the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI   MEPC 83 meeting preview Watch a video IMO GHG Strategy SDGs IMO e-Learning TC Portal PUBLICATIONS International Maritime Organization (IMO) 4 Albert Embankment, London SE1 7SR, United Kingdom +44 (0) 20 7735 7611 +44 (0) 20 7735 7611 info@imo.org IMO in the UN Member States Affiliated Bodies and Programs Circulars Conventions IMO FAQ Careers at IMO Internships Externships Procurement Casualties National Contacts Publications Online Ordering Certificate Verification LRIT MKC Online Catalogue IMO Web Accounts Documents and Resources Fraud Alert Site Index Contact Us --> Copyright International Maritime Organization (IMO). Marine Pollution Volume 12 - 2025 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2025.1683017 Global coordination and challenges of technical standards and application specifications for marine clean alternative fuels in the IMO’s new emission reduction regulations Shasha Wang 1 Y L Yanan Liu 1 J Z Jinglin Zhang 2 L Z Lifang Zhao 1 X L Xiaofei Liu 1 * 1. School of Law, Weifang University, Weifang, China 2. University of Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom Article metrics View details 1 Citations 2,8k Views 422 Downloads Abstract Introduction: Against the backdrop of intensifying climate change, new emission reduction regulations from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) are driving the shipping industry to accelerate decarbonization. Clean alternative fuels are critical for achieving net-zero emissions; however, the development of their technical standards and application specifications lags behind technological advancements. This study focuses on the standards and specifications for marine clean alternative fuels under IMO’s new regulatory framework, aiming to address global coordination challenges and support the green transition of the shipping industry. Methods​: This research employs a multidimensional approach: systematically reviewing policies and regulations from the IMO and major shipping nations/regions; integrating authoritative data from sources such as DNV GL and Clarksons Research to conduct a life-cycle assessment of mainstream clean alternative fuels; and constructing three representative scenarios through scenario analysis to evaluate fuel competitiveness and the direction of standard development. Results​: The analysis reveals significant disparities in regulatory frameworks: China’s "1+N" policy system emphasizes top-down coordination, the EU relies on carbon trading mechanisms and mandatory measures like FuelEU Maritime, Japan prioritizes safety standards (e.g., ClassNK guidelines), and Singapore adopts pragmatic policies to establish a green fuel hub. Three major challenges in global standard harmonization are identified: geopolitical competition leading to fragmentation of standards, technological innovation outpacing regulatory development, and uneven infrastructure deployment. Discussion: To address these challenges, this study proposes establishing a global multi-level governance system, accelerating the construction of port infrastructure, and promoting the integration of international policies and standards. These measures aim to facilitate the coordinated development of technical standards and application specifications for marine clean alternative fuels, providing a systematic foundation for the industry’s green transition. 1 Introduction Conventional fossil fuels are non-renewable resources. The exhaust gases emitted from ships powered by fossil fuels contain atmospheric pollutants such as sulfur oxides (SO X ) and nitrogen oxides (NO X ), as well as greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ). They not only contribute to air pollution in port areas but also exacerbate global climate change. A report published by Simpson Spence Young (SSY), an independent shipbroker based in the UK, states that global shipping CO 2 emissions increased by 4.9% year over year to 833 million tons in 2021 ( Gas network ). On 13 November 2024, the Global Carbon Budget 2024 Report , led by the University of Exeter and compiled by over 80 institutions, was released at COP29. The report indicates that global CO 2 emissions are likely to hit an all-time high in 2024, pushing the world further off track from meeting critical climate targets, with total emissions expected to reach 41.6 billion tons, up from 40.6 billion tons in 2023. Most of these emissions originate from the combustion of coal, oil, and natural gas ( Global Carbon Project ). Given the depletion of conventional fossil fuels and the pressing need to mitigate climate change, the demand for an energy transition is becoming increasingly urgent, with alternative energy sources emerging as a key solution for shipping decarbonization. Unlike land-based energy transitions, maritime operations face greater challenges due to the involvement of port infrastructure development, international conventions, flag state regulations, port state controls, and fuel supply chains, making the adoption of marine clean alternative fuels more complex ( Molland, 2008 ). To achieve sustainable green development in shipping, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has been actively promoting maritime decarbonization and advocating for the goal of net-zero emissions in international shipping. At its 72 nd Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) session, the IMO set an ambitious target to reduce the annual total greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by at least 50% by 2050 compared to 2008 levels. The 83 rd MEPC session, held in London on 7–11 April 2025, approved draft amendments to Annex VI of the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), marking the world’s first regulatory framework combining mandatory emission limits with greenhouse gas pricing in the shipping industry. This milestone framework represents a crucial step toward achieving net-zero carbon emissions in international shipping around 2050 ( IMO, a ). To meet these emission reduction targets, the shipping market is accelerating research and the application of new energy sources. Energy efficiency and cleanliness are the two core principles guiding the development of future marine fuels. Decarbonization pathways for shipping involve two key approaches: in the short term, improving marine engine technology and combustion efficiency, and in the long term, developing and adopting marine clean alternative fuels ( Li et al., 2025 ). In this global “race to net zero,” major maritime nations strive to lead in new energy, propulsion systems, and materials, seeking a voice in setting international standards and technical regulations to gain strategic advantages for their domestic industries. Liquefied natural gas (LNG), liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), methanol, biofuels, ammonia, hydrogen, nuclear energy and other low- or zero-carbon alternatives are currently the primary types of marine clean alternative fuels. Newer low-carbon auxiliary propulsion technologies include fuel cell systems, energy storage battery systems, and wind-assisted propulsion. When selecting marine clean alternative fuels, shipping companies focus primarily on the integrity of the fuel supply chain, operating costs, and safety. Even though clean alternative fuel technology is still in its infancy, the study and use of marine clean alternative fuels is becoming an unstoppable trend due to stricter emission reduction goals. According to statistics from Clarksons Research (CR), as early as 2021, there were 449 newbuild orders for alternative-fuel vessels worldwide, a significant increase compared with 209 vessels in 2020. In the first quarter of 2022, alternative-fuel vessels accounted for 61% of total newbuild orders by gross tonnage. In terms of fuel types, LNG remains the mainstream alternative, representing 94% of orders by vessel count, followed by methanol dual-fuel vessels (4%) and ethane dual-fuel vessels (2%), with 10% of vessels designed to use both LNG and ammonia ( Eworldship, a ). In 2024, the green and low-carbon trend continued to dominate the shipping market, with the size of the alternative-fuel-powered fleet expanding further and the share of such vessels in newbuild orders rising. By 2024, vessels powered by marine clean alternative fuels accounted for 43.2% of the global fleet by deadweight tonnage, marking a two-percentage-point increase from 2023. From January to April 2025, the share of alternative-fuel newbuild orders rose further to 63%, with orders for conventionally fueled vessels nearly disappearing ( Al-Asmakh et al., 2025 ). These data indicate that, beginning in 2025, the application of marine clean alternative fuels in shipping has entered a new stage of rapid development, accelerating the sector’s decarbonization process ( China Ocean Shipping e-Journal ). As such regulations become more stringent, the use of carbon-neutral fuels will progressively increase, with ammonia and bio methanol considered the most promising options. The growing demand for the application of marine clean alternative fuels has also increased the need for a comprehensive regulatory framework for clean energy in shipping. The international regulatory framework continues to evolve. Several international standards have been successively developed, such as the Generic interim guidelines on Training for Seafarers on Ships Using Alternative Fuels and New Technologies, the Use of Hydrogen as Fuel, Interim Guidelines for the Use of Ammonia Cargo as Fuel, and Interim Recommendations for the Carriage of Liquefied Hydrogen in Bulk the Interim Guidelines for the Safety of Ships Using Methyl/Ethyl Alcohol as Fuel (MSC.1/Circ.1621), and the Interim Guidelines for the Safety of Ships Using Ammonia as Fuel (MSC.1/Circ.1687). Although international regulatory rules for marine clean alternative fuels are being introduced at an accelerated pace, the global adoption of a “dominant fuel” remains contested due to technological and geopolitical factors. These factors further complicate international regulation and the global coordination of standards for marine clean alternative fuels ( Kołakowski et al., 2024 ). Technical standards and regulations for marine clean alternative fuels have not received much in-depth academic research up to this point. sections.md:
MLIT is Japan's lead ministry for land, sea, and air transport infrastructure and policy. Its Maritime Bureau holds regulatory authority over international and coastal shipping, seafarer certification, vessel safety, port-state control, and environmental compliance for shipping operating in Japanese waters.

The Maritime Bureau's English portal confirms Japan's participation as a founding member of an international framework to support shipping with technology challenges, and confirms Japan's public commitment to a net-zero GHG emissions target for global shipping by 2050 — a position Japan stated at IMO MEPC in October 2021.

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau English portal, MLIT, accessed April 2025. Operational implication: [https://www.mlit.go.jp/en/maritime/index.html](https://www.mlit.go.jp/en/maritime/index.html)*

**Why this applies to the workspace:** Workspaces operating as freight forwarders on Asia trade lanes — including Japan origin or destination routing — are affected by MLIT Maritime Bureau regulations in two ways. First, ocean freight carriers calling Japanese ports are subject to Japanese port-state control (PSC) inspections, vessel safety standards, and environmental reporting requirements that flow through to service quality, vessel availability, and routing decisions. Second, *Analytical inference:* Japan's stated alignment with IMO's 2050 net-zero strategy means Japanese-flag vessels and port infrastructure will progressively face tightening requirements consistent with IMO MEPC.377(80), the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy.

*Source: IMO Resolution MEPC.377(80), 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, adopted 7 July 2023. [https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/KnowledgeCentre/IndexofIMOResolutions/MEPCDocuments/MEPC.377(80).pdf](https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/KnowledgeCentre/IndexofIMOResolutions/MEPCDocuments/MEPC.377(80).pdf)*

For the workspace's highest-priority verticals — live events, fine art, high-value automotive, and humanitarian — ocean freight is tertiary by volume but is used for large, heavy, or cost-sensitive consignments. Disruption to Japanese port operations or vessel routing driven by regulatory tightening has a direct effect on lead times and routing options for these shipments.

They are listed here as available-pool sources; their content was not retrieved for this brief and claims from them are not carried forward until retrieved and verified.*

---

## Confirmed from Provided Source

The MLIT Maritime Bureau English portal confirms the following active regulatory and administrative functions relevant to freight forwarders on Japan-connected ocean routes:

**Port-State Control (PSC) inspections:** Japan conducts PSC inspections for vessels calling Japanese ports. The portal lists the Detention List — vessels detained following PSC inspection — as a live publication. Detention of a vessel on a Japan-route directly affects cargo in transit on that vessel, including high-value and time-sensitive verticals (live events equipment, fine art, film and TV production cargo).

- *Cause:* PSC detention of a vessel in a Japanese port.
- *Mechanical consequence:* Cargo aboard that vessel is held pending resolution of the deficiency. Depending on deficiency severity, the vessel may be held for days to weeks.
- *Effect on live events and film/TV verticals:* These verticals carry strict delivery windows tied to production or event schedules. Ocean freight used for set, equipment, or props on Japan-connected legs would face total schedule failure if the carrying vessel is detained. Effect on fine art and humanitarian: reputational and operational disruption. Effect on high-value automotive: financial exposure on consignment value. **The workspace should verify carrier PSC detention history on Japan routes before committing time-sensitive cargo to ocean mode.**

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal, "Contact Information & Detention List in Japan (PSC)," MLIT, accessed April 2025. [https://www.mlit.go.jp/en/maritime/index.html](https://www.mlit.go.jp/en/maritime/index.html)*

**Container loss reporting requirement:** The portal confirms Japan has enacted reporting requirements for loss of freight containers from non-Japanese flag vessels in Japanese coastal waters. This is a direct operational compliance item for ocean freight operations.

- *Cause:* Container loss event in Japanese coastal waters involving a non-Japanese-flag vessel.
- *Mechanical consequence:* Reporting obligation triggered under MLIT Maritime Bureau requirements.
- *Effect on workspace:* As freight forwarder, the workspace is not the vessel operator, but may be the cargo party with reporting or notification obligations to clients and potentially to regulators depending on the role formalization in the booking contract. **Legal Confirmation Required** on freight forwarder notification obligations under the container loss reporting framework.

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal, "Reporting Requirements for Loss of Freight Containers from non-Japanese Flag Vessels in Japanese Coastal Waters," MLIT, accessed April 2025.*

**MLC 2006 compliance publications:** The portal maintains live lists of ships issued Maritime Labour Convention certificates and non-applicability certificates. This is relevant to carrier vetting for humanitarian verticals, where MLC compliance is increasingly a client and donor requirement.

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal, "List of Ships Issued of Maritime Labour Certificate," MLIT, accessed April 2025.*

**IMO 2050 Net-Zero Strategy alignment:** Japan's October 2021 statement at IMO set a net-zero GHG target for global shipping by 2050. This is consistent with IMO MEPC.377(80)'s adopted 2050 net-zero ambition and Japan's role as a founding member of the international framework referenced on the MLIT portal.

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal press release, "Japan sets a target for global shipping of achieving net-zero GHG emissions by 2050," 26 October 2021; IMO MEPC.377(80), July 2023.*

## Not Confirmed from Provided Source

The following are **research gaps** pending primary source retrieval:

- GX-ETS mandatory compliance threshold, timeline, and covered entity scope
- GX-Surcharge (carbon levy) introduction date and rate
- Truck driver overtime cap (2024 Problem) specific regulatory instrument and freight impact data
- Hydrogen port development program (facility names, timelines, funding status)

These should be retrieved from the MLIT 2nd Basic Plan on Transport Policy and Japan's GX legislative documentation before being used in briefings or client conversations.

---

**MONITORING — Japan–IMO 2050 Net-Zero Alignment, Ocean Routing Review**

- **Action:** Review ocean freight carrier panel for Japan-connected routes and confirm which carriers hold or are pursuing compliance posture consistent with IMO MEPC.377(80). This is directly relevant to tertiary ocean mode for high-value automotive and large live events cargo routed via Japan.
- **Cost:** Effect on freight rates from IMO-aligned fuel transition is not quantifiable from available sources at this time. Directionally, Japanese-flag and Japanese-port-calling carriers are expected to face compliance cost increases as IMO CII ratings tighten post-2026. Operational implication: *Cost impact requires carrier-specific data.*
- **Who is affected:** Operations and commercial leads managing Japan-origin or Japan-transit ocean freight bookings across all verticals.
- **Why now:** Japan has publicly aligned with net-zero 2050 at IMO and participates in the international framework for shipping technology challenges. Carrier compliance differentiation on Japan routes will become visible in rate structures and service availability ahead of IMO enforcement milestones. Early carrier conversations provide lead time.

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal, MLIT, April 2025; IMO MEPC.377(80), July 2023.*

---

**MONITORING — GX-ETS and Road Freight Capacity Claims: Research Gap**

The existing brief preview contains specific claims about Japan's GX Emissions Trading Scheme (mandatory from 2026, 100,000-tonne threshold) and the 2024 truck driver overtime cap ("2024 Problem"). These claims are **not grounded in the provided source content** (the MLIT Maritime Bureau landing page). They may be accurate but require verification against primary MLIT policy documents or authoritative secondary sources before the workspace relies on them operationally or in client conversations.

- **Action:** Retrieve and verify the GX-ETS legislative instrument and the MLIT 2nd Basic Plan on Transport Policy (available at the MLIT policy document URL in the available sources pool) before using GX-ETS timelines in client communications or supply chain planning.
- **Who is affected:** Commercial leads using Japan decarbonisation claims in client conversations; operations leads planning road freight capacity on Japan-connected inland movements.

*Source gap: GX-ETS specific thresholds and dates not confirmed by provided source content. MLIT 2nd Basic Plan on Transport Policy (FY2021–2025) is available in the sources pool at [https://www.mlit.go.jp/sogoseisaku/transport/content/001578180.pdf](https://www.mlit.go.jp/sogoseisaku/transport/content/001578180.pdf) and should be retrieved for verification.*

*Source: MLIT, "Outline of 2nd Basic Plan on Transport Policy (FY2021–2025)." [https://www.mlit.go.jp/sogoseisaku/transport/content/001578180.pdf](https://www.mlit.go.jp/sogoseisaku/transport/content/001578180.pdf)*

Operational implication: This document covers the Japan Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT) Maritime Bureau's regulatory activity as it applies to freight forwarding operations on Japan-connected trade lanes, with specific relevance to workspaces operating air-primary, road-secondary, and ocean-tertiary transport with live events, fine art, luxury goods, film and TV, high-value automotive, and humanitarian cargo verticals.

The document is anchored to the MLIT Maritime Bureau's published English-language portal. Where the source confirms a policy position, it is reported. Where the existing brief preview contained claims the provided source does not support, those claims are withheld and flagged as research gaps requiring sourced verification before use.

**Convention note:** All cost and rate figures are sourced where available. Unsourced figures are labeled. Items requiring legal review are labeled "Legal Confirmation Required." Dates are sourced; projected dates are labeled as such.

---

**PSC detention monitoring:** The workspace should implement a standing check of the MLIT Maritime Bureau Detention List before finalising ocean freight bookings on Japan-connected routes for time-sensitive cargo verticals (live events, film and TV, fine art). This is a low-cost operational step with direct protective value.

- *Scope:* Ocean freight bookings, Japan origin or transit.
- *Deadline:* Immediate — no regulatory deadline; operational risk is current.
- *Gap from current baseline:* If the workspace does not currently run a PSC detention check as part of carrier vetting on Japan routes, this is a gap. The detention list is publicly available on the MLIT portal.

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal, accessed April 2025.*

**Carrier IMO CII rating awareness:** As IMO CII rating tightening progresses post-2026, carriers on Japan routes will face operational constraints (speed reductions, route modifications, vessel retirement) that affect service quality. The workspace should begin collecting CII rating data from its Japan-route ocean carrier panel to anticipate service disruption risk.

- *Scope:* All ocean freight bookings, Japan-connected routes.
- *Deadline:* No current regulatory deadline on the workspace. IMO CII rating enforcement on carriers has been in effect since 1 January 2023; annual ratings are published.
- *Gap from current baseline:* If the workspace does not currently track carrier CII ratings, this is a gap that will become commercially material as D- and E-rated vessels face operational restrictions.

*Source: IMO MEPC.377(80), July 2023; MLIT net-zero alignment, October 2021.*

- 2024 truck driver overtime cap regulatory instrument date (unverified from provided source)

*Sources: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal, April 2025; IMO MEPC.377(80), July 2023.*

---

No direct registration or reporting obligations on freight forwarders are confirmed from the provided source content. Vessel operators calling Japanese ports hold the PSC compliance and detention-risk exposure.

**Research gap:** Whether Japan's emerging carbon pricing framework (GX-ETS) creates indirect data-supply or reporting obligations for freight forwarders handling Japanese-origin or Japan-transit cargo — including Scope 3 emissions data requests from covered companies — is not determinable from the provided source. **Legal Confirmation Required** once the GX-ETS primary legislative text is retrieved and verified.

---

As a freight forwarder — not a vessel operator, shipowner, or cargo principal — the workspace does not hold direct compliance obligations under MLIT Maritime Bureau vessel safety, environmental, or seafarer regulations. Those obligations sit with the vessel operators and Japanese-flag carriers.

The workspace's compliance chain position on Japan-connected ocean freight is as follows:

- **Vessel operators and carriers** hold the primary obligations: CII rating compliance, port-state control compliance, MLC 2006 certification, and (as they develop) GHG reporting under IMO and any Japanese domestic scheme.
- **The workspace, as freight forwarder,** holds an indirect exposure through carrier selection, routing decisions, and client commitments on sustainability. Where carriers face compliance cost increases, those costs are typically passed through in rate structures.
- **Legal Confirmation Required:** Whether Japan's domestic carbon pricing scheme (GX-ETS, if enacted as described in the existing brief preview) imposes any indirect reporting or data-supply obligations on freight forwarders acting as agents for cargo — including Scope 3 supply chain reporting obligations — requires legal review against the enacted GX-ETS legislative text, which has not been confirmed from the provided source.

*Source: MLIT Maritime Bureau portal, April 2025; IMO MEPC.377(80), July 2023.*

Organization (IMO or the Organization) is the United Nations specialized agency responsible for safe, secure and efficient shipping and the prevention of pollution from ships. 1.2 The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships (the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy) represents the continuation of work by IMO as the appropriate international body to address greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from international shipping. This work includes Assembly resolution A.963(23) on IMO policies and practices related to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from ships, adopted on 5 December 2003, urging the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC or the Committee) to identify and develop the mechanisms needed to achieve the limitation or reduction of GHG emissions from international shipping. 1.3 In response to the Assembly's request, work to address GHG emissions from ships has been undertaken by the Organization, as summarized in appendix 1. 1.4 The Initial IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships (resolution MEPC.304(72)) was the first milestone set out in the Road map for developing a comprehensive IMO strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships (the Road Map) approved at MEPC 70. The Road Map identified that a revised strategy was to be adopted in 2023. 1.5 The adoption of the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy is the latest milestone set out in the Road Map. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy also sustains the momentum and represents the continuation of work by IMO as the appropriate international body to address GHG emissions from international shipping. Context 1.6 The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy falls within a broader context that includes: .1 other existing instruments related to the law of the sea, including UNCLOS, and to climate change, including the UNFCCC and its related legal instruments, including the Paris Agreement; 2 the leading role of the Organization in the development, adoption and assistance in implementation of environmental regulations applicable to international shipping; .3 the decision of the thirty-second session of the Assembly (A 32) in December 2021 that adopted for the Organization a strategic direction entitled "Respond to climate change"; and .4 the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Emissions and emission scenarios 1.7 The Third IMO GHG Study 2014 estimated that GHG emissions from international shipping in 2012 accounted for some 2.2% of anthropogenic CO2 emissions and that such emissions could grow by between 50% and 250% by 2050.RESOLUTION MEPC.377(80) (adopted on 7 July 2023) 2023 IMO STRATEGY ON REDUCTION OF GHG EMISSIONS FROM SHIPS MEPC 80/17/Add.1 Annex 15, page 5 I:\MEPC\80\MEPC 80-17-Add.1.docx 1.8 The Fourth IMO GHG Study 2020 estimated that GHG emissions from shipping in 2018 accounted for some 2.89% of global anthropogenic GHG emissions and that such emissions could represent between 90% and 130% of 2008 emissions by 2050. 1.9 Future annual IMO emission and carbon intensity estimates using the available data from the IMO Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Database (IMO DCS) and other relevant sources would help reduce the uncertainties associated with these emission estimates and scenarios. Objectives of the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy 1.10 The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy is aimed at: .1 enhancing IMO's contribution to global efforts by addressing GHG emissions from international shipping. International efforts in addressing GHG emissions include the Paris Agreement and its goals and the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its SDG 13: "Take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts"; .2 identifying actions to be implemented by the international shipping sector, as appropriate, while addressing impacts on States and recognizing the critical role of international shipping in supporting the continued development of global trade and maritime transport services; and .3 identifying actions and measures, as appropriate, to help achieve the above objectives, including incentives for research and development and monitoring of GHG emissions from international shipping. 2 VISION IMO remains committed to reducing GHG emissions from international shipping and, as a matter of urgency, aims to phase them out as soon as possible, while promoting, in the context of this Strategy, a just and equitable transition. 3 LEVELS OF AMBITION, INDICATIVE CHECKPOINTS, AND GUIDING PRINCIPLES Levels of ambition 3.1 Subject to amendment depending on reviews to be conducted by the Organization in accordance with section 7, the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy identifies levels of ambition for the international shipping sector noting that technological innovation and the global introduction and availability of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and/or energy sources for international shipping will be integral to achieving the overall level of ambition. 3.2 The levels of ambition and indicative checkpoints should take into account the well-to-wake GHG emissions of marine fuels as addressed in the Guidelines on life cycle GHG intensity of marine fuels (LCA guidelines) developed by the Organization1 with the overall objective of reducing GHG emissions within the boundaries of the energy system of international shipping and preventing a shift of emissions to other sectors. 1 Resolution MEPC.376(80)RESOLUTION MEPC.377(80) (adopted on 7 July 2023) 2023 IMO STRATEGY ON REDUCTION OF GHG EMISSIONS FROM SHIPS MEPC 80/17/Add.1 Annex 15, page 6 I:\MEPC\80\MEPC 80-17-Add.1.docx 3.3 Levels of ambition directing the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy are as follows: .1 carbon intensity of the ship to decline through further improvement of the energy efficiency for new ships to review with the aim of strengthening the energy efficiency design requirements for ships; .2 carbon intensity of international shipping to decline to reduce CO2 emissions per transport work, as an average across international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030, compared to 2008; .3 uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and/or energy sources to increase uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and/or energy sources to represent at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030; and .4 GHG emissions from international shipping to reach net zero to peak GHG emissions from international shipping as soon as possible and to reach net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e. close to, 2050, taking into account different national circumstances, whilst pursuing efforts towards phasing them out as called for in the Vision consistent with the long-term temperature goal set out in Article 2 of the Paris Agreement. Indicative checkpoints 3.4 Indicative checkpoints to reach net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping: .1 to reduce the total annual GHG emissions from international shipping by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, compared to 2008; and .2 to reduce the total annual GHG emissions from international shipping by at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040, compared to 2008. Guiding principles 3.5 The principles guiding the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy include: .1 the need to be cognizant of the principles enshrined in instruments already developed, such as: .1 the principle of non-discrimination and the principle of no more favourable treatment, enshrined in MARPOL and other IMO conventions; and .2 the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances, enshrined in UNFCCC, its Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement;RESOLUTION MEPC.377(80) (adopted on 7 July 2023) 2023 IMO STRATEGY ON REDUCTION OF GHG EMISSIONS FROM SHIPS MEPC 80/17/Add.1 Annex 15, page 7 I:\MEPC\80\MEPC 80-17-Add.1.docx .2 the requirement for all ships to give full and complete effect, regardless of flag, to implementing mandatory measures to ensure the effective implementation of this Strategy; .3 the need to consider the impacts of measures on States, including developing countries, in particular on LDCs and SIDS, and their specific emerging needs, as recognized in the Revised Strategic Plan for the Organization (resolution A.1149(32)); and .4 the need for evidence-based decision-making balanced with the precautionary approach as set out in resolution MEPC.67(37). 4 CANDIDATE SHORT-, MID- AND LONG-TERM GHG REDUCTION MEASURES WITH POSSIBLE TIMELINES AND THEIR IMPACTS ON STATES Timelines 4.1 Candidate measures set out in this 2023 IMO GHG Strategy should be consistent with the following timelines: .1 short-term GHG reduction measures are the measures finalized and agreed by the Committee between 2018 and 2023, as included in appendix 1; .2 the basket of mid-term GHG reduction measures should be finalized and agreed by the Committee by 2025. In the FY2026, which started in April 2026, the GX-ETS transitioned to a mandatory baseline-and-credit system. Under the GX-ETS, allowances are traded on the market. Upper and lower price limits apply. From FY2033, auctioning will be introduced for high-emitting corporations in the power sector. More than 700 companies, accounting for over 50% of national GHG emissions, participated in the voluntary ETS. Japan combines several carbon pricing instruments to help achieve net zero emissions by 2050: an existing carbon tax, the ETS, and a carbon levy (GX-Surcharge) to be introduced from 2028 on fossil fuel importers and domestic fossil fuel extractors. Plans for this are outlined in the Basic Plan for the “Green Transformation (GX) Policy”, Japan’s ten-year decarbonization strategy. Japan is actively participating in international carbon markets. Its Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) is a bilateral scheme to incentivize decarbonizing technologies and mitigation actions in 31 partner countries. JCM credits are eligible for use in the GX-ETS. Separately, 90 partner countries and over 300 organizations have joined Japan’s global capacity-building initiative, the Article 6 Implementation Partnership. Year in Review The mandatory GX-ETS began in April 2026, following a three-year voluntary phase and the adoption of the “Amended GX Promotion Act” by the Upper House of the Parliament in May 2025. Over the course of 2025, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) held several working group meetings to consult stakeholders on various design aspects of the mandatory GX-ETS such as benchmarks and grandfathering for setting the baselines and upper and lower price limits of emission allowances. Penalties and enforcement If the required number of allowances cannot be surrendered, a payment equal to the shortfall in emission allowances × upper price × 1.1 must be made. Market Regulation Market Stability Provisions INSTRUMENT NAME: N/A Instrument type: Price-based instrument Functioning: When allowance prices rise above an established upper price limit, entities can meet their obligations by paying the upper limit. Upper price limit in FY2027: JPY 4300 (USD 28.73) When a certain number of days pass with trading prices below the lower limit, a reverse auction will be held to balance the supply and demand for allowances. Lower price limit in FY2027: JPY 1700 (USD 11.36) Other Information Institutions involved Ministry of the Environment: Administers the J-Credit and JCM schemes; tasked with developing carbon pricing in Japan jointly with METI. Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI): Administers the implementation of the J-Credit and JCM schemes; responsible for the GX League; tasked with developing carbon pricing in Japan jointly with the Ministry of Environment. Central Environment Council: Advisory body to the Japanese Cabinet. GX Acceleration Agency : Established to carry out operations related to the ETS and the GX-Surcharge system. Press Release：Japan sets a target for global shipping of achieving net-zero GHG emissions by 2050 - MLIT Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism HOME > Japan sets a target for global shipping of achieving net-zero GHG emissions by 2050 Japan sets a target for global shipping of achieving net-zero GHG emissions by 2050 2021/10/26 Japan aims to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from international shipping by 2050. Japan will propose to the IMO that this target should be set as a common level of ambition for the global shipping sector. [Backgrounds] CO2 emissions from international shipping account for about 2.1% of the global total (as of 2018), and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) is taking measures to reduce these emissions. In 2018, the IMO adapted “the INITIAL IMO STRATEGY ON REDUCTION OF GHG EMISSIONS FROM SHIPS” including the following level of ambition and vision. (1) To reduce CO2 emissions per transport work, as an average across international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030; (2) To reduce the total annual GHG emissions by at least 50% by 2050 compared to 2008; and (3) To phase out GHG emissions as soon as possible in this century However, as the world needs to accelerate its efforts to tackle climate change, international shipping is also expected to pursue further efforts to reduce and phase out GHG emissions in order to achieve the temperature goals of the Paris Agreement. [Net-zero GHG emissions by 2050] On 26th October, Mr. Tetsuo Saito, the Minister of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism expressed that “Japan aims to achieve net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by 2050.” At the 77th session of the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 77) to be held in November, Japan will jointly propose with Costa Rica, Norway, the United States, and the United Kingdom that this target should be set as a common level of ambition. Japanese government will also promote development and demonstration of zero-emission ships such as hydrogen-fueled ships or ammonia-fueled ships, which are essential to realize the target. sections.md:
Verify cargo manifests and customs documentation against the amended import prohibition, which was materially broadened by Lei nº 15.088/2025.

FACT: "É proibida a importação de resíduos sólidos e de rejeitos, inclusive de papel, derivados de papel, plástico, vidro e metal." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 49, as amended by Lei nº 15.088/2025. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: The prior text of Art. 49 prohibited only import of "resíduos sólidos perigosos e rejeitos" and those whose characteristics cause damage. The 2025 amendment broadened the prohibition to all solid waste and rejects, naming paper, paper derivatives, plastic, glass, and metal explicitly. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 49 as shown in primary source. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: Two exceptions apply: (§1º) "a importação de resíduos utilizados na transformação de materiais e minerais estratégicos, inclusive aparas de papel de fibra longa, nos termos de regulamento, e de resíduos de metais e materiais metálicos"; and (§2º) "o importador ou o fabricante de autopeças, exceto de pneus, são autorizados a importar resíduos sólidos derivados de produtos nacionais previamente exportados, para fins exclusivos de logística reversa e reciclagem integral, ainda que classificados como resíduos perigosos, nos termos de regulamento." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 49, §§1º–2º, as amended. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Operational implication:* Workspaces handling trans-border movements of recycled or secondary materials (e.g., scrap metal, waste plastics, used electronics) into Brazil face heightened customs risk under the broadened prohibition. Shipments that formerly qualified as permitted recycled-material imports may now be prohibited absent the strategic-materials or automotive-reverse-logistics exemption.

## 1. Shared Lifecycle Responsibility Framework (Arts. 30–31)

FACT: Art. 30 institutes shared lifecycle responsibility "a ser implementada de forma individualizada e encadeada, abrangendo os fabricantes, importadores, distribuidores e comerciantes, os consumidores e os titulares dos serviços públicos de limpeza urbana e de manejo de resíduos sólidos."

The objective of this shared responsibility includes: FACT: "compatibilizar interesses entre os agentes econômicos e sociais e os processos de gestão empresarial e mercadológica com os de gestão ambiental, desenvolvendo estratégias sustentáveis; promover o aproveitamento de resíduos sólidos, direcionando-os para a sua cadeia produtiva ou para outras cadeias produtivas; reduzir a geração de resíduos sólidos, o desperdício de materiais, a poluição e os danos ambientais." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Arts. 30–31. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 2. Mandatory Reverse Logistics — Art. 33 (Core Obligation)

### Six Mandatory Product Categories

FACT: The six product/packaging categories for which reverse logistics is mandatory (Art. 33, caput) are: (I) agrochemicals, their residues and packaging, as well as other products whose packaging constitutes hazardous waste after use; (II) batteries (pilhas e baterias); (III) tyres (pneus); (IV) lubricating oils, their residues and packaging; (V) fluorescent lamps (sodium vapour, mercury, and mixed-light); (VI) electronics and their components. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

### Extension to Additional Packaging

FACT: "Na forma do disposto em regulamento ou em acordos setoriais e termos de compromisso firmados entre o poder público e o setor empresarial, os sistemas previstos no caput serão estendidos a produtos comercializados em embalagens plásticas, metálicas ou de vidro, e aos demais produtos e embalagens, considerando, prioritariamente, o grau e a extensão do impacto à saúde pública e ao meio ambiente dos resíduos gerados." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33, §1º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: Qualification on extension: "A definição dos produtos e embalagens a que se refere o §1º considerará a viabilidade técnica e econômica da logística reversa, bem como o grau e a extensão do impacto à saúde pública e ao meio ambiente dos resíduos gerados." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33, §2º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

### Consumer Return Obligation

FACT: "Os consumidores deverão efetuar a devolução após o uso, aos comerciantes ou distribuidores, dos produtos e das embalagens a que se referem os incisos I a VI do caput, e de outros produtos ou embalagens objeto de logística reversa, na forma do §1º." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33, §4º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

### Chain Return Obligation

FACT: "Os comerciantes e distribuidores deverão efetuar a devolução aos fabricantes ou aos importadores dos produtos e embalagens reunidos ou devolvidos na forma dos §§3º e 4º." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33, §5º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: "Os fabricantes e os importadores darão destinação ambientalmente adequada aos produtos e às embalagens reunidos ou devolvidos, sendo o rejeito encaminhado para a disposição final ambientalmente adequada, na forma estabelecida pelo órgão competente do Sisnama e, se houver, pelo plano municipal de gestão integrada de resíduos sólidos." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33, §6º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

### Information Obligation

FACT: "Com exceção dos consumidores, todos os participantes dos sistemas de logística reversa manterão atualizadas e disponíveis ao órgão municipal competente e a outras autoridades informações completas sobre a realização das ações sob sua responsabilidade." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33, §8º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 3. Packaging Design Requirements (Art. 32)

FACT: Packaging obligations are on "todo aquele que: I - manufatura embalagens ou fornece materiais para a fabricação de embalagens; II - coloca em circulação embalagens, materiais para a fabricação de embalagens ou produtos embalados, em qualquer fase da cadeia de comércio." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 32, §3º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

Qualifications: FACT: "O regulamento disporá sobre os casos em que, por razões de ordem técnica ou econômica, não seja viável a aplicação do disposto no caput." This creates a regulatory exception pathway for technically or economically infeasible cases. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 32, §2º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 4. Waste Classification System (Art. 13)

The law classifies waste by origin and hazardousness. FACT: Classification by origin includes: (a) domiciliary (residential); (b) urban cleaning (public street cleaning); (c) urban solid waste (combining a and b); (d) commercial establishments and service providers; (e) public sanitation services; (f) industrial; (g) health services; (h) civil construction; (i) agrosilvopastoral; (j) transport services (ports, airports, customs terminals, road and rail terminals, border crossings); (k) mining. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 13, I. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: Classification by hazardousness: (a) perigosos (hazardous) — those exhibiting characteristics of "inflamabilidade, corrosividade, reatividade, toxicidade, patogenicidade, carcinogenicidade, teratogenicidade e mutagenicidade" presenting significant public health or environmental risk per law, regulation, or technical standard; (b) não perigosos (non-hazardous) — all others. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 13, II. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Operational implication:* Workspaces operating at ports, airports, or customs terminals (Art. 13, I, j) generate "resíduos de serviços de transportes" — a defined waste category. This classification may trigger waste management plan obligations under Art. 20, IV.

## 5. Hazardous Waste Operators — Special Requirements (Arts. 37–40)

FACT: "A instalação e o funcionamento de empreendimento ou atividade que gere ou opere com resíduos perigosos somente podem ser autorizados ou licenciados pelas autoridades competentes se o responsável comprovar, no mínimo, capacidade técnica e econômica, além de condições para prover os cuidados necessários ao gerenciamento desses resíduos." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 37. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: Legal persons operating with hazardous waste in any phase of management are obligated to register in the "Cadastro Nacional de Operadores de Resíduos Perigosos" (National Registry of Hazardous Waste Operators). FACT: "Para o cadastramento, as pessoas jurídicas referidas no caput necessitam contar com responsável técnico pelo gerenciamento dos resíduos perigosos, de seu próprio quadro de funcionários ou contratado, devidamente habilitado, cujos dados serão mantidos atualizados no cadastro." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Arts. 38–39. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Operational implication:* For workspaces handling dangerous goods — particularly in the automotive, industrial, or humanitarian verticals — the hazardous waste provisions may require registration and a qualified technical responsible party if their Brazilian operations involve managing hazardous waste streams.

## 6. Prohibited Disposal and Import Conduct (Arts. 47–49)

### Prohibited Disposal Forms

FACT: "São proibidas as seguintes formas de destinação ou disposição final de resíduos sólidos ou rejeitos: I - lançamento em praias, no mar ou em quaisquer corpos hídricos; II - lançamento in natura a céu aberto, excetuados os resíduos de mineração; III - queima a céu aberto ou em recipientes, instalações e equipamentos não licenciados para essa finalidade; IV - outras formas vedadas pelo poder público." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 47. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: Exception for open burning: "Quando decretada emergência sanitária, a queima de resíduos a céu aberto pode ser realizada, desde que autorizada e acompanhada pelos órgãos competentes do Sisnama, do SNVS e, quando couber, do Suasa." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 47, §1º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

### Prohibited Import (as amended)

FACT: Current text as amended by Lei nº 15.088/2025: "É proibida a importação de resíduos sólidos e de rejeitos, inclusive de papel, derivados de papel, plástico, vidro e metal." Two exceptions apply as noted above. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 49 as amended. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 7. Priority Hierarchy for Waste Management (Art. 9)

FACT: "Na gestão e gerenciamento de resíduos sólidos, deve ser observada a seguinte ordem de prioridade: não geração, redução, reutilização, reciclagem, tratamento dos resíduos sólidos e disposição final ambientalmente adequada dos rejeitos." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 9º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: Qualification on energy recovery: "Poderão ser utilizadas tecnologias visando à recuperação energética dos resíduos sólidos urbanos, desde que tenha sido comprovada sua viabilidade técnica e ambiental e com a implantação de programa de monitoramento de emissão de gases tóxicos aprovado pelo órgão ambiental." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 9º, §1º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 2. Annual Reporting by Hazardous Waste Operators

FACT: Legal persons operating with hazardous waste are required to: "informar anualmente ao órgão competente do Sisnama e, se couber, do SNVS, sobre a quantidade, a natureza e a destinação temporária ou final dos resíduos sob sua responsabilidade." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 39, §2º, II. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 3. Waste Management Plan Reporting System

FACT: "Os responsáveis por plano de gerenciamento de resíduos sólidos manterão atualizadas e disponíveis ao órgão municipal competente, ao órgão licenciador do Sisnama e a outras autoridades, informações completas sobre a implementação e a operacionalização do plano sob sua responsabilidade." FACT: "Para a consecução do disposto no caput, sem prejuízo de outras exigências cabíveis por parte das autoridades, será implementado sistema declaratório com periodicidade, no mínimo, anual, na forma do regulamento." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 23, caput and §1º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 4. SINIR — National Solid Waste Information System

FACT: "A União, os Estados, o Distrito Federal e os Municípios organizarão e manterão, de forma conjunta, o Sistema Nacional de Informações sobre a Gestão dos Resíduos Sólidos (Sinir), articulado com o Sinisa e o Sinima." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 12. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 1. Waste Management Plan — Content and Technical Responsible Party

FACT: For entities subject to Art. 20, the waste management plan must contain as minimum: description of the operation; diagnosis of solid waste generated (origin, volume, characterization, environmental liabilities); identification of responsible parties per waste management stage; definition of operational procedures; identification of shared/consortium solutions; preventive and corrective actions for mismanagement accidents; targets for minimization, reuse, and recycling; measures addressing environmental liabilities; periodic revision schedule. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 21. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: "Para a elaboração, implementação, operacionalização e monitoramento de todas as etapas do plano de gerenciamento de resíduos sólidos, nelas incluído o controle da disposição final ambientalmente adequada dos rejeitos, será designado responsável técnico devidamente habilitado." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 22. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Operational implication:* Workspaces operating Brazilian facilities (warehouses, freight terminals) that generate non-domestic-equivalent or hazardous waste must designate a qualified technical responsible party. This requires identifying a duly qualified person — from in-house staff or external contract — before the plan is submitted.

## 2. Reverse Logistics System Infrastructure

FACT: Art. 33 §3º specifies that obligated parties may, among other measures: "I - implantar procedimentos de compra de produtos ou embalagens usados; II - disponibilizar postos de entrega de resíduos reutilizáveis e recicláveis; III - atuar em parceria com cooperativas ou outras formas de associação de catadores de materiais reutilizáveis e recicláveis, nos casos de que trata o §1º." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 33, §3º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Operational implication:* Workspaces assisting clients in structuring reverse logistics compliance can position themselves as logistics partners for the collection, transport, and return of in-scope products — a commercial opportunity alongside the compliance obligation.

## 3. Reverse Logistics Credit Mechanism

FACT: BVRio, in collaboration with the National Association of Catadores, developed in 2012 a Reverse Logistics Credits Mechanism to assist companies to meet their obligations under the law while rewarding Catadores for their role. FACT: "Reverse Logistics Credits are certificates that confirm that reverse logistics services were provided to ensure that a certain amount of waste was responsibly disposed of. These credits are issued and sold by cooperatives of Catadores and purchased by producers and/or importers who need to comply with the solid waste legislation." *Source: Circular Action Hub, Brazilian Solid Waste Legislation. https://www.circularactionhub.org/certification/brazilian-solid-waste-legislation/

*Operational implication:* For clients facing reverse logistics obligations, the credit mechanism provides a compliance pathway without requiring direct investment in collection infrastructure. Workspaces advising clients on Brazilian market entry can flag this mechanism as an operational alternative.

## 4. Waste Transport Manifesto (MTR)

FACT: Decree No. 10.936/2022 introduced the MTR as "a self-declared document valid throughout the national territory, aimed at ensuring the environmental monitoring of Reverse Logistics Systems." *Source: Mondaq/KLA Advogados, Reverse Logistics: Regulatory Decrees And The Role Of The States, 4 October 2024. https://www.mondaq.com/brazil/waste-management/1526446/reverse-logistics-regulatory-decrees-and-the-role-of-the-states

*Operational implication:* Any workspace arranging transport of solid waste, recyclable materials, or post-consumer returns within Brazil requires MTR documentation per Decree 10.936/2022. This is an operational system requirement for any Brazilian domestic logistics involving waste streams.

## 5. Hazardous Waste: Insurance and Technical Capacity

FACT: "No licenciamento ambiental de empreendimentos ou atividades que operem com resíduos perigosos, o órgão licenciador do Sisnama pode exigir a contratação de seguro de responsabilidade civil por danos causados ao meio ambiente ou à saúde pública, observadas as regras sobre cobertura e os limites máximos de contratação fixados em regulamento." Qualification: "O disposto no caput considerará o porte da empresa, conforme regulamento." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 40. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## Extended Producer Responsibility Frameworks

FACT: The PNRS "paved the road for the development of Extended Producer Responsibility schemes in the country, as it establishes shared responsibility for the product life cycle (Art. 30) and determines the obligation of reverse logistics for generating companies (Article 33)." *Source: Circular Action Hub, Brazilian Solid Waste Legislation. https://www.circularactionhub.org/certification/brazilian-solid-waste-legislation/

## Waste Picker Integration as Compliance Pathway

FACT: "There are close to one million catadores in the country, many of which organized into hundreds of co-operatives and associations. While in the past, the remuneration of catadores was derived only from the sale of the recyclable materials collected, the PNRS established the basis for the remuneration for the environmental services of reverse logistics." *Source: Circular Action Hub, Brazilian Solid Waste Legislation. https://www.circularactionhub.org/certification/brazilian-solid-waste-legislation/

*Industry interpretation:* The catador cooperative system is a recognised, regulator-endorsed compliance mechanism. Workspaces with clients facing reverse logistics obligations — particularly for packaging, electronics, or consumer goods — can point to Reverse Logistics Credit purchases from catador cooperatives as both a compliance tool and a social value proposition in client communications.

## Academic Research on PNRS Implementation

FACT: A peer-reviewed study (Trigo et al., 2023) in the *Latin American Journal of Management for Sustainable Development* analysed Decree 10.936/2022 and found the principal results include "the evaluation of potential gains of scale and use of synergies of reverse logistics systems, respecting the effectiveness of the national information system on solid waste management for management continuous improvement" and noted that "the social contribution is the effective closure of all dumps and controlled landfills." *Source: Inderscience, Latin American Journal of Management for Sustainable Development, Vol.6 No.1, 2023. https://www.inderscience.com/info/inarticle.php?artid=132353

*Analytical inference:* Academic evidence suggests the Decree 10.936/2022 framework has scale-efficiency gains as a design objective — meaning compliance through collective/consortium reverse logistics arrangements (rather than individual systems) is both legally permitted and policy-encouraged. This is commercially relevant for workspaces proposing shared logistics solutions to clients.

## Circular Economy Integration

FACT: The PNRS "helps understand the impacts of the production process, not only in the use of raw materials, but also at the end of the life cycle for products consumed in the market. With instruments that establish a hierarchy of activities and priority for the prevention and reduction of waste generation, it promotes the concept of circular design." *Source: Enel Américas, Regulations on the National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS), 11 February 2022. https://www.enelamericas.com/en/circular-economy-latam/articles/regulations-on-the-national-solid-waste-policy-PNRS-and-creation-of-the-national-inverse-logistics-program.html

| October 2025 | Decree 12.688/2025 — regulates Art. 32 §1º (packaging) and Art. 33 §1º (packaging reverse logistics extension) | In force | Assess new packaging obligations |

*Source for all timeline entries: Lei nº 12.305/2010 full text; Câmara dos Deputados legislative record. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm; https://www2.camara.leg.br/legin/fed/lei/2010/lei-12305-2-agosto-2010-607598-norma-pl.html

## Penalty Summary

FACT: "Sem prejuízo da obrigação de, independentemente da existência de culpa, reparar os danos causados, a ação ou omissão das pessoas físicas ou jurídicas que importe inobservância aos preceitos desta Lei ou de seu regulamento sujeita os infratores às sanções previstas em lei, em especial às fixadas na Lei nº 9.605, de 12 de fevereiro de 1998, que 'dispõe sobre as sanções penais e administrativas derivadas de condutas e atividades lesivas ao meio ambiente, e dá outras providências', e em seu regulamento." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 51. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: The law specifically amended Lei nº 9.605/1998, Art. 56 §1º, adding criminal liability for those who "manipula, acondiciona, armazena, coleta, transporta, reutiliza, recicla ou dá destinação final a resíduos perigosos de forma diversa da estabelecida em lei ou regulamento." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 53. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: "A observância do disposto no caput do art. 23 e no §2º do art. 39 desta Lei é considerada obrigação de relevante interesse ambiental para efeitos do art. 68 da Lei nº 9.605, de 1998, sem prejuízo da aplicação de outras sanções cabíveis nas esferas penal e administrativa." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 52. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Analytical inference:* The PNRS does not set out a standalone penalty tariff — it cross-references Brazil's Environmental Crimes Law (Lei 9.605/1998), which provides both administrative fines and criminal sanctions. Specific fine amounts under Lei 9.605 and its implementing decree (Decreto 6.514/2008) are not within the corpus sourced content.

Specific penalty quantum (fine amounts): *Specific administrative fine amounts not available from primary PNRS sources as of July 2026. Amounts are governed by Lei nº 9.605/1998 and Decreto nº 6.514/2008 — Brazilian environmental counsel should confirm applicable sanctions.*

---

## Electronics and Components

FACT: Electronics and their components are a mandatory reverse logistics category (Art. 33, VI). FACT: "A logística reversa relativa aos produtos de que tratam os incisos V e VI do caput do art. 33 será implementada progressivamente segundo cronograma estabelecido em regulamento." Items V (fluorescent lamps) and VI (electronics) are subject to progressive implementation per regulatory schedule. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 56. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

FACT: Decree No. 10.240 of 12 February 2020 regulates Art. 33, caput, VI and Art. 56 (electronics and progressive implementation). *Source: Câmara dos Deputados, Lei nº 12.305/2010 — Dados da Norma. https://www2.camara.leg.br/legin/fed/lei/2010/lei-12305-2-agosto-2010-607598-norma-pl.html

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating in electronics freight forwarding or import, the progressive implementation schedule for electronics reverse logistics is active. The relevant implementing decree (10.240/2020) and subsequent decrees (11.413/2023) establish operational timelines and verification mechanisms.

## Automotive / Lubricating Oils and Tyres

FACT: Both lubricating oils (their residues and packaging) and tyres are mandatory reverse logistics categories (Art. 33, IV and III respectively). These are not subject to the "progressive implementation" carve-out in Art. 56 (which applies only to V and VI). *Analytical inference:* Full reverse logistics obligation for these categories is immediately active without a progressive phase-in.

## Packaging in General

*Analytical inference:* The extension of reverse logistics to plastic, metal, and glass packaging under Art. 33 §1º via sectoral agreements or decrees — with Decree 12.688/2025 now in force — creates a broadening compliance perimeter for workspaces whose clients use such packaging for goods sold in Brazil.

---

## 1. Radioactive Waste Exclusion

FACT: "Esta Lei não se aplica aos rejeitos radioativos, que são regulados por legislação específica." Complete exclusion — no PNRS obligations attach to radioactive waste. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 1º, §2º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 2. Mining Waste — Open-Air Disposal Exception

FACT: Art. 47, II prohibits open-air disposal "excetuados os resíduos de mineração" — mining waste is explicitly carved out from the open-air disposal prohibition. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 47, II. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 3. Commercial Waste Equiparated to Domiciliary Waste

FACT: "Respeitado o disposto no art. 20, os resíduos referidos na alínea 'd' do inciso I do caput [commercial establishment waste], se caracterizados como não perigosos, podem, em razão de sua natureza, composição ou volume, ser equiparados aos resíduos domiciliares pelo poder público municipal." Qualification: this applies only if characterised as non-hazardous and only by municipal authority decision. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 13, parágrafo único. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Operational implication:* If a workspace's Brazilian office or small operations generate non-hazardous commercial waste, there may be a pathway for municipal equiparation to domiciliary waste, reducing compliance burden. This is determined by municipal authority.

## 4. Simplified Waste Management Plan for Micro and Small Enterprises

FACT: "Serão estabelecidos em regulamento: [...] II - critérios e procedimentos simplificados para apresentação dos planos de gerenciamento de resíduos sólidos para microempresas e empresas de pequeno porte, assim consideradas as definidas nos incisos I e II do art. 3º da Lei Complementar nº 123, de 14 de dezembro de 2006, desde que as atividades por elas desenvolvidas não gerem resíduos perigosos." Qualification: the simplified procedure is not available if the enterprise generates hazardous waste. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 21, §3º, II. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 5. Art. 49 Import Prohibition — Two Statutory Exceptions

As noted above: (1) strategic materials and long-fibre paper offcuts per regulatory definition; (2) auto parts importers/manufacturers for products previously exported from Brazil, for exclusive reverse logistics and integral recycling purposes. *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 49, §§1º–2º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

## 6. Sectoral Agreements and Terms of Commitment

FACT: Sectoral agreements and terms of commitment can have national, regional, state, or municipal scope. FACT: "Os acordos setoriais e termos de compromisso firmados em âmbito nacional têm prevalência sobre os firmados em âmbito regional ou estadual, e estes sobre os firmados em âmbito municipal." FACT: "Na aplicação de regras concorrentes consoante o §1º, os acordos firmados com menor abrangência geográfica podem ampliar, mas não abrandar, as medidas de proteção ambiental constantes nos acordos setoriais e termos de compromisso firmados com maior abrangência geográfica." *Source: Lei nº 12.305/2010, Art. 34, §§1º–2º. https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2010/lei/l12305.htm

*Operational implication:* Where a client sector has a national-level sectoral agreement, that agreement governs reverse logistics obligations in that sector regardless of state law — unless the state law is more stringent. Workspaces advising clients must identify the applicable sectoral agreement tier.

Law that regulates the National Policy on waste management in Brazil and that establishes principles, objectives, instruments and guidelines for the integrated management of solid waste. Its principles include sustainable development; eco-efficiency reducing the environmental impact; the recognition of recyclable solid waste as an economic good and of social value; shared responsibility for the product life cycle; and eco-labeling and sustainable consumption. The law paved the road for the development of Extended Producer Responsibility schemes in the country, as it establishes shared responsibility for the product life cycle (Art. 30) and determines the obligation of reverse logistics for generating companies (Article 33). The law, consequently, creates legal obligations on solid waste collection and appropriate destination (i.e., reverse logistics) that apply to producers, importers, retailers and distributors from seven industrial sectors (tyres, lubricating oils, batteries, pesticides, fluorescent lamps, electric and electronic products) and packaging in general (which may involve different sectors and approaches). Furthermore, the PNRS requires the integration of waste pickers in the process (Art. 7), as this informal sector has a key role in waste management in the Brazilian scenario (as in development countries in general). Waste pickers in Brazil are known as “catadores”, low-income groups that make a living by collecting recyclable materials in the streets, rubbish dumps and landfills. There are close to one million catadores in the country, many of which organized into hundreds of co-operatives and associations. While in the past, the remuneration of catadores was derived only from the sale of the recyclable materials collected, the PNRS established the basis for the remuneration for the environmental services of reverse logistics. Given the above, the PNRS is considered here as a standard in itself for the Waste Management Sector in Brazil, complemented by specific state and municipal regulations. The PNRS provides flexibility as to how companies can demonstrate compliance, and different approaches have been proposed and adopted by industry, including the use of reverse logistics credits. REVERSE LOGISTICS CREDITS FOR COMPLIANCE WITH THE PNRS In order to facilitate compliance with the PNRS, BVRio in collaboration with the National Association of Catadores, developed in 2012 a Reverse Logistics Credits Mechanism to assist companies to meet their obligations under the law while rewarding Catadores for their role. Reverse Logistics Credits are certificates that confirm that reverse logistics services were provided to ensure that a certain amount of waste was responsibly disposed of. These credits are issued and sold by cooperatives of Catadores and purchased by producers and/or importers who need to comply with the solid waste legislation. Through the purchase of credits, companies effectively subcontract cooperatives of Catadores to provide reverse logistics services. The sale of Reverse Logistics Credits does not affect the ability of the Catadores to sell the physical material to be recycled and, indeed, these are often sold to different parties and create an additional revenue stream to them (see more info in the Knowledge Hub ). In order to monitor the performance of the operations of these cooperatives, BVRio developed a system to collect and store the electronic invoices/receipts associated with all transactions involving recyclable waste materials. Such invoices (called ‘Nota Fiscal Eletrônica’ – “NFs”) are linked to the Brazilian Tax & Revenue system and therefore difficult to forge, and contain all information related to a transaction, including the names of buyer and seller, the types of material, quantities and price. Associated with other checks and balances, these provide an effective framework for a reverse logistics credit system. NFS AS PROTO-CREDITS Since this approach was developed and adopted by BVRio, there has been a vibrant market for NFs, that act as proto-credits for solid waste recycling. Market participants using solely NFs, however, lack additional safeguards and verifications, making the system potentially open for abuse. While Circular Action Hub accepts this compliance mechanism as a tool for meeting the objectives of the Brazilian legislation, it recommends that buyers certify their activities to one the voluntary credit systems recognised by the Hub so to add extra layers of social and environmental robustness to their transactions.
