Brazil Environment Flávia Marcilio and José Davi Fidalgo To print this article, all you need is to be registered or login on Mondaq.com. Article Insights This article from KLA Advogados is most popular: within Environment topic(s) in South America Flávia Marcilio’s articles from KLA Advogados are most popular: in South America with readers working within the Retail & Leisure industries KLA Advogados are most popular: within Transport, Food, Drugs, Healthcare, Life Sciences and Consumer Protection topic(s) As we mentioned in the last blog post , regarding Law No. 12.305/2010 , which established the PNRS (National Solid Waste Policy), we will now discuss two important decrees on the subject: Decree No. 10.936/2022 , which regulates the National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS), and Federal Decree No. 11.413/2023 , which further expands on the PNRS. The Regulatory Decree No. 10.936/2022 established: The National Reverse Logistics Program, integrated with the National Information System on Solid Waste Management (Sinir) and the National Solid Waste Plan (Planares), and The waste transport manifesto (MTR), a self-declared document valid throughout the national territory, aimed at ensuring the environmental monitoring of Reverse Logistics Systems. Additionally, the decree provides specific treatment for hazardous waste and mandates that the reverse logistics system for pesticides, their residues, and packaging will be addressed in specific legislation. Decree 11.413/2023 deepens and elaborates on Law 12.305/2010, known as the National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS). This law established the general framework for solid waste management in Brazil, including reverse logistics. It defined the principles, objectives, and tools for implementing public solid waste policies, but left several aspects to be regulated through decrees and other complementary norms. Objective : Enhance the implementation and operation of physical and logistical infrastructure for recycling, promote collaboration between reverse logistics and recycling systems, and encourage the reuse of solid waste. Recycling Incentives : It promotes the use of materials with a lower environmental impact, the development of more recyclable products, and the inclusion of waste pickers and cooperatives in the recycling chain. Transparency and Traceability : Implements an electronic information system (black box) to track the amount of products and packaging recycled and ensure transparency in the process. Governance : Defines the responsibilities of managing entities, companies, and result verifiers, and establishes monitoring and control mechanisms. Decree 11.413/2023 is designed to detail and operationalize the provisions of the PNRS related to reverse logistics. CCRLR (Reverse Logistics Recycling Credit Certificate): Confirms the return of products or packaging to the production cycle. CERE (General Packaging Structuring and Recycling Certificate): Certifies companies that invest in structured projects for the recovery of recyclable materials. Future Mass Credit Certificate: Allows companies to meet reverse logistics goals in advance by investing in long-term projects. Federal Government Ordinance Recently, at the beginning of August, the federal government issued Ordinance GM/MMA No. 1117, which regulates Decree No. 11.413/2023 to establish criteria for the qualification of result verifiers in reverse logistics systems and initiate the first public call for registration of legal entities with the Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change (MMA). In summary, the ordinance requires that legal entities contracted by managing entities submit a request to the MMA, which will analyze, qualify, and later publish it in Sinir. Entities responsible for managing information related to the reverse logistics system include legal entities registered under the CNPJ, as well as foreign companies authorized to operate in Brazil. Among the provisions, verifiers must not have direct relationships with manufacturers, importers, distributors, or retailers connected to the reverse logistics system being verified, as well as representative entities, managing entities, or third parties involved in operating the system. Furthermore, verifiers must issue an annual report to the MMA, providing the results of the managing entities. Additionally, special attention is given to verifying, validating, and authenticating the electronic invoices issued by operators and generated in the operation/commercialization of products and packaging, to ensure the effective return of recyclable materials to the production cycle for reuse. Entities must adapt to the conditions of the Ordinance within 180 days of its publication. The qualification will be valid for 3 years from the date of the act's publication and can be renewed for equal periods, provided that the entity submits a request to the MMA 90 days before the expiration date and continues to meet the qualification criteria. It is important to note that a lack of qualification does not prevent result verifiers from performing their activities in reverse logistics systems, as long as they comply with state and municipal regulations. State Regulations Currently, 13 states have reverse logistics policies established by law: São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Paraná, Piauí, Pernambuco, Paraíba, Maranhão, Sergipe, Amazonas, Goiás, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, and Rio Grande do Sul. This means that companies that import, manufacture, distribute, or market products and/or packaging sold in these states must comply with current legislation regarding reverse logistics, even if they are not based in those states. On a state level, in addition to the highlight for Mato Grosso do Sul mentioned in our Environmental Law team's alert, we also highlight the regulations developed by São Paulo. In São Paulo, Law No. 12.300/2006 established the State Solid Waste Policy and was regulated by State Decree No. 54.645/2009 . Although these regulations do not specifically address Reverse Logistics, they recognize the post-consumer responsibility of producers, importers, transporters, distributors, retailers, consumers, waste pickers, collectors, administrators, and other operators involved in any phase of solid waste management. The SMA Resolution No. 45/2015 established guidelines for implementing and operationalizing post-consumer responsibility in the state of São Paulo. Who is Subject In São Paulo, those obligated to establish a Reverse Logistics system, through the return of products and packaging after consumer use, are "the manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers of products that, due to their characteristics, require or may require special systems for packaging, storage, collection, transportation, treatment, or final disposal to prevent harm to the environment and public health (...)" (Art. 2). The resolution lists products and packaging sold in São Paulo that are subject to the Reverse Logistics system: Among the products that result in waste considered to have significant environmental impact are: lubricating oil, cooking oil, automotive oil filters, automotive batteries, portable batteries, electronic products and their components, fluorescent lamps (sodium, mercury vapor, and mixed light), unusable tires, household medications (expired or unused); and Among the packaging for products that make up the dry fraction of urban solid waste or equivalent (excluding those classified as hazardous by Brazilian law) are: food, beverages, personal hygiene products, perfumes and cosmetics, cleaning products and related items, other utensils and consumer goods, in addition to packaging containing pesticides and automotive lubricating oil. Commitment Agreements It is possible to enter into Commitment Agreements with the Secretariat of Environment, Infrastructure, and Logistics of the State of São Paulo (SEMIL) and the Environmental Company of the State of São Paulo (CETESB), as well as linking the renewal of operating licenses issued by the agency. Commitment Agreements are not explicitly defined in regulations but are referred to as an option in the absence of a sectoral agreement for the product or when stricter commitments need to be established. They must be approved by the competent environmental agency. In these cases, either party may sign an individual Commitment Agreement, and the instrument may have state-level applicability (Art. 32, Federal Decree 7.404/2010 ), allowing for technical and economic evaluation by the States. The Commitment Agreement is also established as an instrument of PERS (Art. 4, Section VI, State Law 12.300/2006 ), but without a specific definition in regulation. Failure to comply with the Resolution may result in penalties provided for in environmental legislation, particularly in State Laws No. 9.509/1997 and No. 12.300/2006, State Decree No. 54.645/2009, and Federal Decree No. 6.514/2008. The content of this article is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter. Specialist advice should be sought about your specific circumstances. Article: Reverse logistics: Brazilian national policy on solid waste from Decree 10,936/2022 perspective Journal: Latin American Journal of Management for Sustainable Development (LAJMSD) 2023 Vol.6 No.1 pp.45 - 59 Abstract: The National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS) came to define responsibilities for collaborative actions. Decree No. 10,936/2022 brought new regulations that promote the implementation of reverse logistics systems. The present work aims to discuss the impacts of the new PNRS regulation regarding reverse logistics. Documentary research was carried out for subsequent content analysis process, through investigation and examination of the legal decree. As main results, it is indicated the evaluation of potential gains of scale and use of synergies of reverse logistics systems, respecting the effectiveness of the national information system on solid waste management for management continuous improvement. These theoretical-methodological contributions are still incipient. However, the social contribution is the effective closure of all dumps and controlled landfills. This gap appears as an opportunity for studies, considering that the reality of solid waste management in Brazilian municipalities is heterogeneous. With mandatory inverse logistics, companies will have to rethink their production strategy, logistics, and durability of products, and even communication with their customers, expanding the foundation for education aimed at conscious consumerism and circular economy. The importance of waste management The regulations on solid waste management have grown significantly since 2010 in Brazil, with the National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS) as a legal framework that provides incentives for the implementation of Circular Economy. This is because it helps understand the impacts of the production process, not only in the use of raw materials, but also at the end of the life cycle for products consumed in the market. With instruments that establish a hierarchy of activities and priority for the prevention and reduction of waste generation, it promotes the concept of circular design. It also clearly values the pillars of Circular Economy in its orientation: Prioritize non-generation; Develop means for reduction; Reuse; Recycling; Treatment; Environmental rational final disposal. This legal framework supports cities’ transition process to a circular economy model, as it creates circular disposal mechanism for this waste, which allows for the development of new businesses and the reduction in demand for natural resources. Moreover, it stimulates a new more sustainable way of thinking about society. Inverse logistics This concept determines that manufacturers, importers, distributors, sellers, consumers, and public solid waste management and trash collection services are responsible for the life cycle of their products. The shared responsibility is applied both individually and throughout the chain. That is, when producing and selling a product, the company is not exempt from responsibility for its impact at the end of its life cycle. For a country of continental proportions, the importance of a policy focused on inverse logistics represents a strategic element that favors the creation of reception, treatment, and distribution centers. This helps reduce the fundamental logistical obstacles to the expansion of a circular economy. Therefore, one important tool is an instrument for the coordination and integration of inverse logistics systems in order to help achieve results across the different systems implemented or in process across the country. It is also important to improve communication with citizens regarding voluntary drop-off points for the adequate disposal of waste, which ensures traceability of materials. The regulations on the PNRS were an important legislative milestone for Brazil to continue moving forward in its actions aimed at circularity. However, one of its greatest potentials is to expand the notion of society consumption and circularity of materials. Twitter LinkedIn © Enel Américas 2016 Legal Notice Ethical Channel

**Stated 2030 deadline and scale target.** The coalition's collective commitments are described as representing "an estimated annual demand of $16 billion by 2030" and "31 million tonnes (Mt) CO2e in annual emissions reductions" once purchasing commitments are met. *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

**Offtake activity as of January 2024.** "FMC members have been involved in 94 offtake agreements or investment projects to secure emerging climate technologies and near-zero emission goods and services from qualified suppliers." *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

**The acceleration gap.** The AFSA source notes that "the Mission Possible Partnership's Global Project Tracker reveals, however, that the heavy industry transition needs to accelerate sevenfold to meet 2030 climate targets." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

**CDR purchasing shortfall.** As of mid-2024, "advance purchases for engineered CDR are only at a total of about 11 million tonnes — a minuscule fraction of what is needed." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

**The stated technology rationale.** "Half of the emissions reductions needed by 2050 must come from technologies not yet available at scale." *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

*Analytical inference:* The conversion trigger from voluntary signal to active commercial pressure for logistics operators is the point at which FMC members embed their procurement commitments in supply-chain contract clauses — specifically, minimum-percentage thresholds for near-zero emission shipping, SAF-blended air freight, or low-emission trucking. The AFSA source confirms the mechanism is already operating in shipping through ZEMBA: Amazon is "supporting joint efforts under ZEMBA to ship 600,000 TEUs on zero-emission vessels over three years." When anchor shippers of this scale attach near-zero conditions to freight tender documents, carriers without compliant capacity are excluded from bid lists — and forwarders without carrier access to compliant capacity face the same exclusion downstream.

*Analytical inference:* The sevenfold acceleration gap noted above, combined with the 2030 deadline, indicates that the gap between stated demand and available supply is the dominant near-term constraint, not demand. For freight-sector suppliers (carriers, forwarders), this is simultaneously a competitive risk (clients with FMC commitments cannot be served without near-zero capacity) and a commercial opportunity (first movers in compliant capacity win preferred-supplier status while scarcity persists).

---

**Aviation / SAF.** The AFSA source states that "sustainable aviation fuel can cost five times more than traditional jet fuels." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

*Operational implication:* For workspaces moving high-value or time-critical cargo by air — including live events, fine art, film and TV, and luxury goods verticals where air is the primary mode — FMC-driven SAF commitments by airline members translate into surcharge pass-through risk on affected routes. Clients who are themselves FMC members (or who have adopted comparable sustainability commitments under peer pressure from FMC members in their supply chain) may request SAF-blended shipments. At a five-times cost premium, this is a material line item on time-critical air freight invoices and a pricing conversation that requires advance preparation.

*Operational implication:* The UpLink-FMC Sustainable Aviation Challenge identified 16 start-up finalists from over 130 applicants working on SAF production efficiency, battery-powered flight, and hydrogen flight. *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/ These represent emerging supplier options that are pre-commercial scale. Workspaces cannot yet procure from these sources at volume, but tracking finalist companies is forward positioning for when commercial supply emerges.

**Shipping / zero-emission maritime.** Zero-emission fuels for shipping are described as "currently cost three to four times the price of bunker fuel." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

*Operational implication:* For workspaces using ocean freight on secondary or tertiary lanes — including bulky equipment for live events or automotive — the ZEMBA 600,000-TEU zero-emission block procurement by Amazon and co-buyers is a market-structure event, not just a corporate announcement. When large shippers block-book compliant capacity, spot availability for non-members on those lanes tightens, and rate premiums on remaining green capacity increase. The workspace should monitor which carriers are the ZEMBA vessels, and whether its ocean lane pricing reflects early green-capacity scarcity.

**Trucking / CDR.** The source set does not provide a current cost figure for zero-emission trucking or drayage under the FMC framework beyond "trucking is expected to double by mid-century" in demand terms. *Specific current cost differential for FMC-compliant zero-emission trucking not available from primary sources as of 2025.*

---

**Action 1 — Map carrier access to FMC-compliant capacity.** Identify which of the workspace's primary air and ocean carriers participate in FMC, ZEMBA, or equivalent near-zero capacity programmes. Carriers with FMC-aligned capacity can be presented to clients with FMC commitments as compliant options. This is a carrier-relationship audit, not a procurement change, and requires no capital outlay.

**Action 2 — Access the First Suppliers Hub.** Review the First Suppliers Hub (launched January 2024) to identify which suppliers in aviation, shipping, and trucking are listed as meeting FMC commitment thresholds. Use this as a screening list when responding to client RFPs that include near-zero emission freight requirements. *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

**Action 3 — Add SAF cost framing to client pricing conversations.** The five-times SAF cost premium is a publicly sourced figure. For air-primary verticals (live events, fine art, film/TV, luxury goods, high-value automotive) where clients may carry FMC commitments or face shareholder pressure toward them, prepare a cost scenario illustrating the SAF surcharge range at current premiums. This positions the workspace as informed rather than reactive when clients ask.

**Action 4 — Track the 2026 FMC Impact Brief for delivery data.** The January 2026 Impact Brief confirms active monitoring of delivery against commitments. When the full brief content becomes publicly available (the source set carries only the publication listing and abstract), it will be the primary source for updated offtake data, sector-by-sector progress, and any threshold revisions. Set a retrieval trigger for Q1 2026 report body and Q1 2027 annual update.

**Action 5 — Monitor ZEMBA capacity allocation on affected ocean lanes.** For the workspace's ocean freight activity, identify whether lanes used by the workspace intersect with those where ZEMBA block-book commitments concentrate. If Amazon and co-buyers are pre-purchasing zero-emission capacity on specific corridors (likely transpacific and Europe–Asia given shipping demand volumes), the workspace should assess whether its spot or contract capacity access on those corridors is affected by green-capacity scarcity.

*No capital commitment or contract change is recommended at this stage. This is a positioning and monitoring action set. Severity: MONITORING.*

---

**First Suppliers Hub as a procurement filter.** In January 2024, "the FMC launched the First Suppliers Hub, a global repository of innovative and emerging technologies and suppliers that are working to meet the FMC commitment thresholds across several key high-emissions sectors. The hub features more than 80 decarbonization efforts that are currently underway." *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

*Analytical inference:* The First Suppliers Hub functions as a preferred-supplier directory for FMC buyers. Freight and logistics operators — whether carriers, forwarders, or NVOCCs — whose services are not listed or who cannot demonstrate alignment with FMC commitment thresholds are invisible to this buyer cohort's procurement process. The workspace should determine whether any of its carrier partners appear in the hub, and whether its own service proposition is presentable in near-zero terms.

**Named competitor context.** The source set does not name direct freight-forwarding or logistics competitors and their FMC positioning. *Specific competitor positioning within the freight forwarding segment is not available from primary sources as of the source dates.*

*Analytical inference:* The named corporate members — DP World Limited and Hanwha Ocean — are logistics-sector companies with direct FMC membership. DP World's membership as a port and logistics operator, and Hanwha Ocean's membership as a shipbuilder, signal that the FMC's influence is reaching infrastructure and capacity layers of the freight sector, not only cargo principals. Workspaces operating as freight forwarders between these infrastructure players and the cargo-owner members face positioning pressure from both ends of the chain.

**CDR market concentration.** Microsoft alone accounts for "more than 60 percent of all engineered CDR purchases made to date." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition 

*Analytical inference:* CDR market concentration in a single buyer creates fragility for the supply side. For workspaces whose clients include technology-sector shippers with high Scope 3 ambitions, the Microsoft precedent is a conversation reference — but the workspace should not overstate CDR's near-term operational relevance to freight services. CDR commitments in the FMC framework relate to carbon removal credits, not to freight emission intensity.

| 2 | Decarbonizing Industry Through Demand: The First Movers Coalition | Industry/Policy Analysis | American Foreign Service Association / Foreign Service Journal | September 2024 | https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition |
| 3 | First Movers Coalition Impact Brief 2026 | Institutional Publication | World Economic Forum | 19 Jan 2026 | https://www.weforum.org/publications/first-movers-coalition-impact-brief-2026/ |
| 4 | First Movers Coalition: Introduction & Overview – WTO Presentation | Intergovernmental Presentation | World Economic Forum / WTO TESSD | March 2025 | https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tessd_e/11_subsidies_presentation_by_wef.pdf |

*Note: The BCG source (https://www.bcg.com/publications/2023/harnessing-purchasing-power-drive-deep-decarbonization-first-movers-coalition) and the two WEF FMC home pages (https://initiatives.weforum.org/first-movers-coalition/home and https://weforum.org/first-movers-coalition) returned only cookie-consent and navigation content in the source blocks provided. No substantive claims were drawn from these three sources. They are listed here for registry completeness but not cited in the brief body.*

---

## New Sources Identified

| Source Name | URL | Tier estimate (1-7) | Why this source matters |
|-------------|-----|---------------------|------------------------|
| First Movers Coalition: Introduction & Overview – WTO Presentation (March 2025) | https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tessd_e/11_subsidies_presentation_by_wef.pdf | 2 | Intergovernmental body context: WEF presenting FMC at WTO TESSD suggests coalition is engaging trade-policy forums on subsidy and market-access dimensions; this source likely contains participant lists, threshold definitions, and policy asks not available in the press-release sources. |

---

The co-founding institutions are the World Economic Forum and the United States government. Former US Special Presidential Envoy for Climate John Kerry became co-chair and, per the AFSA source, "continues to drive this initiative forward, rallying top companies with high climate ambition and a willingness to harness their purchasing power to decarbonize heavy-emitting industries." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

Member companies make purchasing commitments described as follows: "Members make purchasing commitments applicable to a minimum percentage of their existing spend on products and services in one or more FMC sectors by 2030 (e.g., 10 percent of the company's steel procured or 10 percent of the volume of goods shipped overseas)." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

Named member companies active as of January 2024 include: Qatar Airways, Velux, The Coca Cola Company, GE Vernova, DP World Limited, Capgemini, Danfoss A/S, Hanwha Ocean, Neutron Holdings (Lime), Volvo Cars, Inc., Chooose AS, Boom Technology, Drax Corporate Limited and Norsk Hydro ASA — described as "the most recent members to join FMC" at that date. *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

Amazon is named as a founding member active in the shipping sector: "Amazon, a founding member of the FMC, has been instrumental in getting the Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) off the ground." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

Microsoft is identified as the dominant buyer in the carbon dioxide removal segment: "Microsoft is leading the charge, accounting for more than 60 percent of all engineered CDR purchases made to date." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

Advisory and implementation partners named in the source set include BCG, Deloitte, RMI (Rocky Mountain Institute), ResponsibleSteel, Greenhouse, and Salesforce. *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

*Analytical inference:* The coalition's strategic intent is to aggregate individually sub-scale procurement signals into a collective demand floor large enough to de-risk capital investment in nascent technologies. The stated mechanism — "FMC members are sending an unprecedented signal of demand, which will serve to drive up investment in and production of the critical emerging technologies" — positions FMC as a market-creation instrument rather than a regulatory compliance body.

*Industry interpretation:* The WTO presentation listed as a corroborating source (March 2025) suggests the coalition has sought to engage intergovernmental trade bodies, likely to address subsidy and trade-policy barriers to near-zero emission goods. This positions FMC participants as policy-influencing actors, not merely buyers.

---

MONITORING

The First Movers Coalition (FMC) is a global public-private partnership described as "a global public-private partnership by the World Economic Forum and the United States government working to decarbonize the world's heavy-emitting sectors." *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

The coalition was launched at COP26 in November 2021, with initial support from 35 global companies. *Source: "Decarbonizing Industry Through Demand: The First Movers Coalition," American Foreign Service Association / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

By January 2024, membership had grown to 96 companies, with "more than 120 commitments to purchase near-zero emission goods and services by 2030." *Source: WEF Press Release, World Economic Forum, 16 January 2024. https://www.weforum.org/press/2024/01/wef24-first-movers-coalition-commitments/

The trigger for accelerating coalition activity is the closing commercialisation window for breakthrough clean technologies. The AFSA source states: "The window is rapidly closing to demonstrate and commercialize these innovative technologies over the critical 2020s decade, so they become available for massive scale-up to enable net-zero emissions by 2050." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

The six hard-to-abate sectors targeted — aluminium, cement and concrete, steel, aviation, shipping, and trucking — "currently account for a third of global emissions" and are "projected to account for 50 percent of emissions by 2050." *Source: AFSA / Foreign Service Journal, September 2024. https://afsa.org/decarbonizing-industry-through-demand-first-movers-coalition

A January 2026 WEF Impact Brief was published specifically to document how "FMC members are delivering on their net-zero commitments within a complex global market," indicating active monitoring of delivery against those commitments. *Source: First Movers Coalition Impact Brief, World Economic Forum, 19 January 2026. https://www.weforum.org/publications/first-movers-coalition-impact-brief-2026/

*Re-check window: The 2026 Impact Brief is the most recent publication available in the source set. Given the coalition's annual Davos cadence, an updated status report or membership announcement is expected at or around the WEF Annual Meeting in January 2027. Set monitor to re-pull Q1 2027.*

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- FMC represents the largest private-sector demand signal for near-zero emission industrial goods and services, with 96 members and $16 billion in stated annual demand by 2030. These are sourced, named figures from a WEF press release dated January 2024.
- Aviation SAF and zero-emission shipping are the two FMC categories with the most direct relevance to freight procurement. SAF currently carries a five-times cost premium over conventional jet fuel; zero-emission marine fuel carries a three-to-four-times premium. These numbers are cited in the September 2024 AFSA/Foreign Service Journal source and should be presented as order-of-magnitude indicators, not precise rate quotes.
- Amazon's ZEMBA commitment — 600,000 TEUs on zero-emission vessels over three years — is a concrete, named, sourced example of how FMC commitments translate into capacity allocation decisions that affect freight markets.

**What to avoid:**

- Do not present FMC membership as a regulatory compliance requirement. It is a voluntary coalition. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any FMC member's procurement commitments, once embedded in a supply contract, create binding obligations on the workspace as a contracted carrier or forwarder requires contract-specific legal review.
- Do not cite the $16 billion annual demand figure as confirmed spend; it is described as an estimate of what commitments "will represent" by 2030, not confirmed contracted volume.
- Do not cite the sevenfold acceleration gap as the workspace's own analysis — it originates from the Mission Possible Partnership's Global Project Tracker, cited in the AFSA source. The workspace has not read that tracker independently.
- Do not claim the workspace's operations are FMC-aligned without being able to identify the specific FMC threshold (e.g., minimum percentage of near-zero emission goods or services in a given sector) that applies and evidence that carrier or supplier contracts meet it.

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- Has your company made FMC purchasing commitments in aviation, shipping, or trucking sectors? If so, what percentage threshold and by when?
- Are you currently procuring SAF-blended freight or zero-emission maritime capacity to fulfil that commitment?
- Does your procurement team require emissions documentation from freight providers to count shipments toward your FMC target?

While no specific WTO agreement focuses solely on the environment, WTO rules allow members to adopt trade-related environmental measures, provided they meet conditions that prevent misuse for protectionist purposes. The WTO contributes to the protection and preservation of the environment through its commitment to sustainable development, its rules and enforcement mechanisms, and the work of its various bodies, in particular the Committee on Trade and Environment . Environment-related WTO videos back to top News back to top Background Trade and Environment at the WTO Introduction History WTO rules and environmental policies Measures aimed at protecting the environment come in various shapes and forms. Under WTO rules, as confirmed by WTO jurisprudence, members can adopt trade-related measures aimed at protecting the environment, subject to certain specified conditions. Introduction Key GATT disciplines GATT exceptions Other relevant WTO texts Environment-related disputes back to top Work in the WTO Trade and Environment Committee The Trade and Environment Committee is the standing forum dedicated to dialogue between governments on the impact of trade policies on the environment, and of environment policies on trade. Created in 1995, the Committee has followed a comprehensive work programme. Under the Doha Development Agenda, the regular committee is also looking at the effects of environmental measures on market access, the intellectual property agreement and biodiversity, and labelling for environmental purposes. Cooperation with Multilateral Environmental Agreements (MEAs) Thematic sessions Trade and Environment Weeks Committee in special session Ministers agreed to negotiate on trade and the environment, with the overarching objective of enhancing the mutual support of trade and environmental policies. Environmental Initiatives Plastics pollution and environmentally sustainable plastics trade Trade and environmental sustainability Fossil fuel subsidy reform Environmental Goods Agreement Separately, eighteen participants representing 46 WTO members are negotiating an Environmental Goods Agreement back to top Topical issues Trade and Climate Change The issue of climate change, per se, is not part of the WTO's ongoing work programme and there are no WTO rules specific to climate change. However, the WTO is relevant because climate change measures and policies intersect with international trade in a number of different ways. Steel Standards Principles The Principles recognize that the iron and steel sector accounts for approximately 8% of annual global greenhouse gas emissions and that these emissions will need to be reduced by at least 90% for the sector to play a credible role in achieving climate targets. They call for establishing common methodologies on measuring greenhouse gas emissions within the iron and steel sector in order to accelerate the transition to near-zero emissions. UN Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs) back to top The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a set of 17 goals and 169 targets that members of the United Nations have endorsed as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. This impact report highlights how First Movers Coalition (FMC) members are delivering on their net-zero commitments within a complex global market. It showcases the successful approaches, emerging trends and concrete solutions that demonstrate how coordinated corporate demand can help shape a net-zero economy. Achieving net zero by 2050 will require the rapid creation of early markets to decarbonize hard-to-abate industries. The private sector has a critical role to play in sending credible demand signals that can unlock investment, accelerate innovation and catalyse supply at scale. The FMC supports the world’s most significant private-sector demand signal for industrial decarbonization. Through collective commitments across seven high-emitting sectors, FMC members are helping to turn ambition into action by backing near-zero technologies and products before they reach full commercial maturity. First Movers Coalition: 120 Commitments for Breakthrough Industrial Decarbonization Technologies > Press releases | World Economic Forum Media News Releases First Movers Coalition: 120 Commitments for Breakthrough Industrial Decarbonization Technologies Published 16 Jan 2024 2024 Share World Economic Forum, public.affairs@weforum.org First Movers Coalition (FMC) reaches 96 members, with more than 120 commitments to purchase near-zero emission goods and services by 2030. These commitments will represent an estimated annual demand of $16 billion by 2030 – the largest demand signal for emerging climate technologies ever created by the private sector. To build on this unprecedented demand, FMC also announces new initiatives to identify the supply of breakthrough decarbonization technologies and to drive investment into industrial decarbonization efforts. Discover more about the First Movers Coalition here . For more information on the Annual Meeting 2024, visit www.weforum.org . Share on social media using the hashtag #wef24. Davos-Klosters, Switzerland, 16 January 2024 – The First Movers Coalition (FMC), a global public-private partnership by the World Economic Forum and the United States government working to decarbonize the world’s heavy-emitting sectors, now represents the world’s largest private sector demand signal for emerging climate technologies with more than 120 commitments from 96 members, the Forum announces today. “The First Movers Coalition is proving the power of private sector cooperation to drive meaningful climate action,” says Børge Brende, President, World Economic Forum. “Together, FMC’s member companies are sending an unprecedented signal of demand, which will serve to drive up investment in and production of the critical emerging technologies needed to decarbonize the most heavy-emitting industrial sectors”. Half of the emissions reductions needed by 2050 must come from technologies not yet available at scale, so creating demand for these technologies will be essential to kickstart the market and catalyse their commercial adoption. To support this, FMC members have collectively made commitments to purchase near-zero emission goods and services that use breakthrough climate technologies by 2030. These commitments cover seven sectors: aluminium, aviation, carbon dioxide removal, cement and concrete, shipping, steel and trucking. By 2030, these commitments will represent an estimated annual demand of $16 billion for emerging climate technologies and 31 million tonnes (Mt) CO2e in annual emissions reductions. “The First Movers Coalition is driving critical progress in the some of the hardest to address sectors,” said John Kerry, US Special Presidential Envoy for Climate. “As members participate in offtake agreements and invest in decarbonization projects in support of their FMC commitments, they continue to give confidence to this market to develop faster. This approach is pivotal in expanding the use and availability of the breakthrough technological solutions that will enable the deep decarbonization of heavy-emitting sectors.” From 35 members when FMC was launched at COP26, the coalition has now reached 96 members and includes some of the world’s largest companies. The most recent members to join FMC are: Qatar Airways, Velux, The Coca Cola Company, GE Vernova, DP World Limited, Capgemini, Danfoss A/S, Hanwha Ocean, Neutron Holdings (Lime), Volvo Cars, Inc., Chooose AS, Boom Technology, Drax Corporate Limited and Norsk Hydro ASA . In just two years, members have also made significant progress on commitments, delivering direct investment in climate technologies and tangible offtakes. As of today, FMC members have been involved in 94 offtake agreements or investment projects to secure emerging climate technologies and near-zero emission goods and services from qualified suppliers. The FMC also announced today several new initiatives focused on identifying the supply of breakthrough decarbonization technologies that will help its members to meet their commitments and to accelerate the pace of investment in industrial decarbonization efforts. These include: Sustainable aviation challenge winners The UpLink-FMC Sustainable Aviation Challenge , in collaboration with Salesforce, multiple industry partners and advisers such as Deloitte, will choose the 16 most innovative start-ups that are accelerating the decarbonization of the aviation industry. Selected from over 130 applicants, the winners champion innovative approaches to sustainable aviation fuel, battery-powered and hydrogen-powered flight. “Air travel is crucial for global connectivity and economic growth, but its environmental impact cannot be ignored. This is why initiatives like the UpLink-First Movers Coalition Sustainable Aviation Challenge are paramount to accelerating climate action. We are proud to support these ecopreneurs who are at the forefront of pioneering innovative climate solutions,” said Suzanne DiBianca, Executive Vice-President and Chief Impact Officer of Salesforce. “Decarbonizing aviation heavily relies on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF); however, the production process is extremely energy intensive,” added Astrid Poupart-Lafarge, President of Energies and Chemicals Segment at Schneider Electric. “We are proud to support emerging technology companies looking to address this challenge through innovation as part of the World Economic Forum’s UpLink challenge. We are ready to collaborate with these top innovators to use our industry-leading energy management and automation technology to enable the necessary design and operational efficiency required to achieve SAF manufacturing at scale.” Near-zero steel 2030 challenge The FMC, in collaboration with Greenhouse and supported by BCG, ResponsibleSteel and RMI, founded as Rocky Mountain Institute, is running a challenge to surface both the supply of and demand for near-zero emissions steel, as well as enabling technologies that could be leveraged to support supply. A total of 67 submissions were received by 10 January 2024 – seven submissions for the supply of near-zero steel and 45 submissions for potential enabling technologies. The challenge also received 15 demand submissions representing an aggregated demand volume of 2.3M tonnes of near-zero steel purchase potential (including from FMC members Bharat Forge, Consolidated Contractors Company, EGUI, General Motors, Invenergy, Johnson Controls, Marcegaglia, Ørsted, ReNew, Vattenfall and the Volvo Group). The challenge is also complementary to RMI’s Sustainable Steel Buyers Platform, which will issue a Request for Proposal to secure low-emission steel offtake agreements in North America. “Leading corporations have the power to send strong demand signals to initiate change in heavy industry, as showcased through First Movers Coalition and the Near Zero Steel Challenge. We are excited to help turn these commitments into offtake agreements through the Sustainable Steel Buyers Platform and our Request for Proposal to North American steelmakers,” said Jon Creyts, Chief Executive Officer of RMI. “By bringing committed buyers together, we can accelerate the investment case for first-of-a-kind, near-zero emissions steel plants and mobilize deep decarbonization of the sector. New sustainable supplier database The FMC launched the First Suppliers Hub , a global repository of innovative and emerging technologies and suppliers that are working to meet the FMC commitment thresholds across several key high-emissions sectors. The hub features more than 80 decarbonization efforts that are currently underway and is open to organizations to leverage as they make progress towards their decarbonization goals. It will continue to grow as more decarbonization efforts are identified that meet the FMC commitment thresholds. “The First Suppliers Hub is a one-of-its-kind, pivotal tool that will accelerate climate action and tap into the immense potential of these emerging technologies that are a crucial component of reaching global decarbonization targets by 2050,” said Jennifer Steinmann, Deloitte Global Sustainability and Climate Practice Leader. “We are proud to be a technical adviser for the creation of the First Suppliers Hub, which will be an invaluable resource to organizations as they move from commitments to action.” New sustainable procurement guide The FMC Cement and Concrete Procurement Guide covers which product category rules (PCRs) should be used as a starting point in order to develop environmental product declarations and reach FMC thresholds. It also provides some clarity on key issues for procurement teams such as how to incorporate carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) in carbon accounting. About the First Movers Coalition The First Movers Coalition seeks to harness the purchasing power of leading global companies to unlock the potential of the emerging technologies needed to decarbonize the world by 2050. The coalition is marshalling leading companies to apply their purchasing power to create guaranteed early markets for advanced technologies to scale up the next generation of net-zero solutions for carbon-intensive sectors. BY PABLO BURKOLTER Following years of insufficient climate action, it is becoming increasingly evident that the Paris Agreement to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius (2°C) and pursue all efforts to limit it to below 1.5°C could be in jeopardy. Every fraction of a degree of warming carries greater risks of cascading climate tipping points, which society must do all it can to mitigate. About 40 percent of the emissions reductions necessary to transition the global economy to net zero by 2050 relies on the development of breakthrough technologies and energy solutions, such as bioenergy, renewable hydrogen-based fuels, green methanol and ammonia, sustainable aviation fuels (SAF), or carbon dioxide removal (CDR)—all of which are at a critical period of early deployment and carry a green premium, a higher cost than traditional technology. The window is rapidly closing to demonstrate and commercialize these innovative technologies over the critical 2020s decade, so they become available for massive scale-up to enable net-zero emissions by 2050. Recognizing the urgency of bringing these technologies to market, President Joe Biden and the World Economic Forum launched the First Movers Coalition (FMC) at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in Glasgow (COP26) in November 2021. The launch was supported by 35 global companies that joined to send a powerful signal that there is firm market demand for the emerging technologies essential for a net-zero transition in “hard-to-abate” sectors. Six economically essential sectors—aluminum, cement and concrete, steel, aviation, shipping, and trucking—currently account for a third of global emissions. If left unabated, these sectors are projected to account for 50 percent of emissions by 2050, driven by a significant increase in global demand estimated at 80 percent for aluminum, 40 percent for cement and concrete, and 30 percent for steel. While sea freight is predicted to triple, trucking is expected to double by mid-century. Stimulation of demand is essential to bring about a systemic change across these sectors and accelerate the pace of the transition to low-carbon solutions. FMC works to create the demand signal needed for technologies to go through the pilot-scale demonstration phase and accelerate the timelines to reach the first go-to-market projects on the path to large-scale commercialization beyond 2030. Former U.S. Special Presidential Envoy for Climate John Kerry became co-chair of the coalition and continues to drive this initiative forward, rallying top companies with high climate ambition and a willingness to harness their purchasing power to decarbonize heavy-emitting industries. FMC and similar coalitions and initiatives that stimulate market demand, accelerate low-carbon technology deployment, and help facilitate bankable offtake agreements are vital to reducing and eliminating the green premium as well as to jump-starting the market for near-zero emissions products and services to achieve the Paris Agreement’s emissions reduction targets. Taking Stock of First Movers in Action Since its launch two years ago, and through the dedicated work of its 100 member companies that have made more than 120 commitments under FMC, the coalition has become the largest private-sector-led global demand signal for products and services made with innovative near-zero emissions technologies and energy solutions. Members make purchasing commitments applicable to a minimum percentage of their existing spend on products and services in one or more FMC sectors by 2030 (e.g., 10 percent of the company’s steel procured or 10 percent of the volume of goods shipped overseas). These procurement figures can be small for a company but represent a substantial demand when aggregating all member commitments. It is estimated that the FMC now represents about $16 billion in aggregate annual demand by 2030, equating to 31 million tons of annual CO2 equivalent emissions reductions once these purchasing commitments are met. FMC has evolved from a purely demand signaling initiative to also support members’ procurement efforts across all seven sectors. The coalition convenes players involved in the full life cycle of a product such as, say, low-carbon aluminum or steel to foster collaboration and action on breakthrough technologies. FMC convenes regional workshops, bringing together experts to discuss scaling up the supply of near-zero emission solutions, identify the challenges and barriers to increasing both demand and supply, and develop concrete recommendations for a way forward. To catalyze the emergence and commercialization of near-zero emissions innovations, the coalition launched two challenges—one on aviation in collaboration with UpLink, the World Economic Forum’s innovation platform, and one on steel in partnership with the Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI) , ResponsibleSteel , and Greenhouse . And in January 2024, the First Suppliers Hub was launched as an online database where current and future suppliers of FMC-compliant technologies can present their products and connect with buyers. Six economically essential sectors—aluminum, cement and concrete, steel, aviation, shipping, and trucking—currently account for a third of global emissions. The value of collaboration has been evident in the past two years. FMC has played an important role in connecting players and creating unconventional partnerships between value chain actors (i.e., those involved in the full life cycle of a product) and other industry sectors to bridge the gaps between demand, supply, and essential ecosystem enablers such as policy, finance, and infrastructure. This has resulted in an increasing number of offtake agreements and investments with suppliers, translating purchasing commitments into action and bringing breakthrough technologies one step closer to commercial scale. For instance, in January 2024, FMC member Ball Corporation announced a collaboration with fellow coalition member Novelis to launch its first-ever low-carbon aluminum cup, made of 90 percent recycled aluminum supplied by Novelis and 10 percent FMC-compliant low-carbon primary aluminum, supplied by Alcoa from the ElysisTM process—an R&D technology that eliminates direct greenhouse gas emissions from the aluminum smelting process. In the aviation sector, where there is already strong demand for sustainable aviation fuels (SAF), public-private partnerships between governments, airlines, fuel suppliers, and investors are needed to expedite its deployment and deliver net-zero aviation. One example of full value chain collaboration that stands out is the Minnesota SAF Hub , where multiple coalition members from different sectors collaborate with the state government and airport to find solutions to scale SAF global production and replace conventional jet fuel. In shipping, Amazon, a founding member of the FMC, has been instrumental in getting the Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) off the ground. Through ZEMBA, cargo owners can demonstrate demand through forward-procurement of zero-emission maritime freight services. Amazon is supporting joint efforts under ZEMBA to ship 600,000 TEUs (20-foot equivalent units) on zero-emission vessels over three years, which will result in close to 1 million tons of CO2 emissions reduction. Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) is increasingly seen as a critical decarbonization tool if we are to hit the Paris climate goals. Up to 10 billion tons of CDR per year is expected to be needed by 2050, according to the median estimates of scenarios considered by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). FMC decided in 2022 to also launch a CDR program under which members commit to contract for at least 50,000 tonnes or $25 million worth of durable and scalable CO2 removal by 2030. To date, while advance purchases for engineered CDR are only at a total of about 11 million tonnes—a minuscule fraction of what is needed—FMC members and implementation partners represent more than 80 percent of that total. Microsoft is leading the charge, accounting for more than 60 percent of all engineered CDR purchases made to date. Among the deals concluded is a 2023 agreement with fellow FMC member Orsted and Aker Carbon Capture, committing to one of the world’s largest carbon removal agreements—2.76 million tonnes of durable CDR over 11 years. These collaborations are a testament to the power that demand signals and early procurement commitments can play in accelerating the deployment of emerging clean energy technologies. The Mission Possible Partnership’s Global Project Tracker reveals, however, that the heavy industry transition needs to accelerate sevenfold to meet 2030 climate targets. To reach FMC’s goals by 2030, the initiatives that FMC members have taken need to be replicated at scale and supported by adequate infrastructure, financing, and an enabling policy environment. The Way Forward FMC’s work has brought to light the challenges of scaling up near-zero emissions products and services, especially at the pace required to get on track for net zero, and the risk that as demand-side signals increase, potential supply shortages might emerge. Some of these challenges are: • Insufficient renewable energy capacity and grid infrastructure to provide the zero-carbon electricity needed to decarbonize (e.g., to produce green hydrogen). • Lack of technology at commercial scale, despite significant progress in developing pathways and pilots that could lead to decarbonization. Will a particular technology prove to be the final pathway, or will it just be transitional, leading to a different path altogether? • Unwillingness to pay for green premiums. Demand remains insufficient, especially at the green premium, to justify the investment required to produce near-zero emissions solutions. For example, zero-emission fuels for shipping currently cost three to four times the price of bunker fuel, while sustainable aviation fuel can cost five times more than traditional jet fuels. • Insufficient collaboration between suppliers, innovators, financiers, demand-side buyers, policymakers, and others in the value chain. Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) is increasingly seen as a critical decarbonization tool if we are to hit the Paris climate goals. To spearhead the shift to near-zero emissions products and services and accelerate the demand for net-zero technologies, additional measures could help us move faster and at scale. First, governments need to enact more supportive policies and regulations that help industry decarbonize, through carbon taxation, tax credits, low-interest loans, subsidies, grants, and other incentives. Policy incentives worth mentioning include the production and investment tax credits envisaged under the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (2022), or the subventions provided under the European Union’s Green Deal Industrial Plan, and the Emissions Trading Scheme. FMC currently has 13 government partners, in addition to the United States, to support efforts on policy and regulations, with more countries interested in partnering, as well. Since public procurement represents a significant share of GDP, the adoption of low-carbon procurement practices could also send a strong market signal to suppliers, incentivize investment and supply chains development, facilitate uptake, and reduce the green premium. In the cement and concrete sector, public procurement is responsible for 40 to 60 percent of global concrete sales, highlighting the impact that public procurement could have. Policy can be leveraged to ensure a broad application of decarbonization targets that can further spur the market by setting mandates for the private sector, for instance. Countries like the United States have signed the Industrial Deep Decarbonisation Initiative (IDDI), co-launched in 2021 by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization and the Clean Energy Ministerial, to tackle carbon-intensive construction materials such as steel, cement, and concrete. But the number of countries signatory to IDDI remains low. Because the breakthrough technologies needed to decarbonize the hard-to-abate industrial sectors require enormous up-front capital investment and ongoing production premiums but are also exposed to operational risks, international financial institutions, domestic development banks, and commercial banks need to cooperate and accelerate efforts to offer financial products that unlock funding and de-risk investments. These may include blended finance, concessionary loans, sustainability bonds, and first-loss insurance. Realizing the Paris Agreement means the so-called hard-to-abate sectors have to abate. sections.md:
## Primary Obligated Parties

The regulation's recitals identify "aircraft operators, airports and other aviation actors" as the parties for whom a level playing field is sought. The regulation targets fuel suppliers and aircraft operators as the primary obligated entities for SAF blending. *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 4, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

## The Workspace's Position in the Chain

*Analytical inference:* A freight forwarder with air as its primary mode sits downstream of the aircraft operator in the compliance chain. The forwarder is neither a fuel supplier nor an aircraft operator. Its direct regulatory exposure under ReFuelEU Aviation is therefore likely limited to: (a) cost absorption or pass-through of SAF premiums embedded in carrier rates; (b) any documentation or sustainability-reporting obligations that flow to shippers or forwarders via carrier-issued SAF certificates or book-and-claim instruments; and (c) disclosure obligations that arise when the workspace makes SAF-related sustainability claims to clients.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a freight forwarder acting as NVOCC-equivalent in air (i.e., consolidating shipments under house airway bills) bears any direct obligation under ReFuelEU Aviation's reporting or accounting provisions requires counsel review of the operative articles.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace's role differs between transactions where it acts as agent for the shipper versus transactions where it acts as principal (e.g., as an air freight consolidator) is a compliance chain question that turns on the operative articles and requires counsel review.

## Cargo Vertical Considerations

*Analytical inference:* For cargo verticals characterised by time-critical or high-value air shipments (live events, fine art, film and TV, high-value automotive, luxury goods, humanitarian), the SAF cost premium is a higher proportion of the total freight cost than for bulk commodities, but represents a smaller proportion of the total shipment value. This asymmetry means that SAF pass-through is commercially manageable for premium verticals but requires transparent documentation to support client sustainability reporting.

---

## SAF Blending Mandate — General Framework

The regulation establishes mandatory SAF uptake obligations. The policy objective is stated in the recitals: "the Union's climate goals" require "a strong ramp-up of the production, supply and uptake of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF)." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 2, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

*Specific [blend percentage targets / escalation schedule / article numbers for the blending mandate] not available from the provided source block text as of 2026-05-27.* The operative blending articles are not reproduced in the source blocks provided. The DG MOVE and IATA corroborating sources (listed in New Sources Identified) are expected to contain this detail and should be retrieved as the priority action.

## Level Playing Field Mechanism

The regulation is explicitly designed to prevent competitive distortion: "it is essential to ensure a level playing field across the Union air transport market regarding aviation fuel." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 5, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng. *Analytical inference:* The level-playing-field mechanism means the regulation applies uniformly across aircraft operators at EU airports, preventing carriers from avoiding SAF costs by re-routing through non-EU hubs — a design feature directly relevant to cargo routing decisions.

## Reporting and Verification

The EASA digital reporting tool page captures active regulatory infrastructure for ReFuelEU Aviation compliance reporting as of April 2026. *Source: EASA ReFuelEU Aviation Digital Reporting Tool page, EASA, last updated 08 April 2026. https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/environment/refueleu-aviation-digital-reporting-tool. The substantive content of that tool — which parties report, what data fields are required, and by what deadlines — is not available from the source block text provided.

*Specific [reporting article / data fields / verification body / submission deadline] not available from primary sources as of 2026-05-27.*

---

## EASA SAF Scale-Up Report

The EASA has published a report on "Sustainable Aviation Fuel scale-up, progress and pressure points," indicating that EASA has assessed current SAF production and supply conditions. *Source: EASA press release, "EASA publishes report on Sustainable Aviation Fuel scale-up, progress and pressure points," EASA, https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/newsroom-and-events/press-releases/easa-publishes-report-sustainable-aviation-fuel-scale-progress. The substantive findings of that report are not available from the source block content provided.

*Analytical inference:* Supply constraints on SAF production are widely discussed in industry reporting. For workspaces relying on air as their primary mode across the Americas and Asia trade lanes, SAF supply shortfalls at specific airports could affect the availability and cost of compliant fuel, translating into carrier surcharge volatility that the workspace should track by route.

## ICAO Traffic Growth Projections

The regulation cites ICAO's post-COVID-19 forecast: "ICAO estimates a growth in Europe of up to 3,1 % per year until 2050 for passenger traffic, and up to 2,4 % per year for freight traffic according to its post-COVID-19 forecast in a high traffic scenario." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 2, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng. *Analytical inference:* Rising air freight volumes at EU airports, combined with a fixed SAF blending obligation, will increase absolute SAF demand and put upward pressure on SAF prices and therefore air freight rates over the medium term.

---

## SAF Cost Tracking

*Analytical inference:* As SAF surcharges are passed through by carriers on EU-departing air freight, the workspace requires a mechanism to capture, record, and report SAF cost components per airway bill or per shipment. Without this, the workspace cannot accurately attribute SAF cost exposure by lane, vertical, or client account, nor can it support client sustainability reporting queries.

## Carrier Documentation Collection

*Analytical inference:* Aircraft operators subject to the SAF blending mandate will generate compliance documentation (SAF certificates, fuel delivery records, potentially CORSIA-linked accounting entries). The workspace, particularly for cargo verticals where clients make sustainability claims, needs a process to request, receive, and archive this documentation. The gap between a manual, relationship-based carrier communication model and a systematic documentation-collection process is operationally significant for high-value and sustainability-conscious cargo verticals.

## Client-Facing Sustainability Reporting Infrastructure

*Analytical inference:* Clients in live events, fine art, luxury goods, film and TV, and humanitarian verticals increasingly require shipment-level carbon and SAF accounting data to satisfy their own sustainability reporting obligations. The workspace needs to be able to receive SAF accounting data from carriers and translate it into per-shipment sustainability metrics for client use. This is an operational system gap that should be addressed before the blending mandate's first reporting cycle.

## CORSIA Intersection

*Analytical inference:* ReFuelEU Aviation intersects with CORSIA (ICAO's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation) for flights on international routes. The regulation's recitals acknowledge ICAO's role: "The Union sustains the efforts made at international, multilateral and bilateral level to promote a high level of ambition and convergence in the uptake of SAF." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 3, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng. For the workspace's international trade lanes (Americas, Asia), the intersection of ReFuelEU Aviation (EU airport departures) and CORSIA (international routes) creates potential dual-framework documentation requirements that should be mapped before the next carrier contract cycle.

---

## Question 1: Does the regulation apply to flights operated by non-EU carriers departing EU airports?

The recitals establish that "intra-EU flights are part of global itineraries set in a global air transport market. The same is valid for itineraries from non-EU to non-EU destinations through European airports." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 4, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the regulation's operative articles apply to non-EU aircraft operators departing EU airports requires review of the operative scope articles, which are not fully available in the provided source blocks.

## Question 2: Does the regulation create direct obligations for freight forwarders?

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the operative articles must be reviewed to determine whether any direct obligation (registration, reporting, documentation, fee payment) attaches to freight forwarders rather than exclusively to aircraft operators and fuel suppliers.

## Question 3: What SAF accounting method governs sustainability claims to clients?

*Analytical inference:* Book-and-claim SAF accounting — where a party purchases a SAF certificate without the physical fuel being loaded on their specific flight — is a live question under ReFuelEU Aviation. Whether the regulation's accounting rules permit book-and-claim for shipper-level sustainability reporting is a threshold question for the workspace's commercial sustainability claims. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the operative articles and any implementing guidance must be reviewed to confirm permissible accounting methods.

## Question 4: What is the penalty for non-compliance?

*Specific [penalty provision / enforcement mechanism / fine quantum] not available from primary sources as of 2026-05-27.* The operative articles carrying the penalty provision are not reproduced in the provided source blocks. This is a required slot gap; see New Sources Identified for retrieval priority.

---

*Specific [exemption provisions / de minimis thresholds / aircraft type or operation exclusions] not available from primary sources as of 2026-05-27.* The operative articles carrying exemption provisions are not reproduced in the provided source blocks. The IATA Handbook (listed in New Sources Identified) is expected to document exemptions and edge cases and should be retrieved as a priority.

*Analytical inference:* Cargo charter operations, humanitarian exemptions, and state aircraft exclusions are standard features of EU aviation regulations. Whether ReFuelEU Aviation contains comparable carve-outs for cargo-only or humanitarian operations is a threshold question for workspaces operating in those verticals.

The EASA digital reporting tool (https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/environment/refueleu-aviation-digital-reporting-tool) represents the live reporting infrastructure, with the page updated as recently as 08 April 2026. *Source: EASA ReFuelEU Aviation Digital Reporting Tool page, EASA, last updated 08 April 2026. https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/environment/refueleu-aviation-digital-reporting-tool.

## What the Regulation Is

Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 — ReFuelEU Aviation — is primary EU legislation adopted on 18 October 2023 and published in the Official Journal of the European Union on 31 October 2023. The regulation's stated purpose is "ensuring a level playing field for sustainable air transport." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

The regulation targets the decarbonisation of air transport through the mandatory uptake of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). The recitals establish the policy rationale: "emissions from air transport have been increasing since 1990 and the trend of increasing emissions could return as we overcome the pandemic. Therefore, it is imperative to prepare for the future and make the necessary adjustments ensuring a well-functioning air transport sector that contributes fully to achieving the Union's climate goals." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 2, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

The regulation connects to the Union's overarching climate architecture: "The Union has established legal obligations under Regulation (EU) 2021/1119 of the European Parliament and of the Council to achieve climate neutrality by 2050 at the latest and to achieve a reduction of net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55 % compared to 1990 by 2030." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 2, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

## Effective Date

The regulation was published in the Official Journal on 31 October 2023. *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, OJ L, 2023/2405, 31.10.2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

*Specific entry-into-force date (typically 20 days after OJ publication) and application date not available from the provided source block text as of 2026-05-27.* Full entry-into-force and first application dates require retrieval of the operative articles; see New Sources Identified.

## Jurisdictional Scope

The regulation applies to the EU air transport market. The recitals describe the aviation market as "one of the most integrated sectors in the internal market, governed by uniform rules on market access and operating conditions." The regulation's EEA relevance is flagged in its title: "(Text with EEA relevance)." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Title and Recital 3, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

*Specific jurisdictional scope article (confirming which flights, airports, and operators are covered) not available from the provided source block text as of 2026-05-27.*

## Why This Regulation Applies to the Workspace

Workspaces operating with air as their primary transport mode move cargo on commercial aircraft departing from EU airports. The regulation imposes SAF blending obligations on aviation fuel suppliers and aircraft operators at EU airports, and introduces reporting and documentation requirements that propagate into the freight value chain. *Analytical inference:* For a freight forwarder whose primary mode is air, the regulation's cost, documentation, and sustainability-reporting implications are direct and near-term: SAF cost premiums are passed through per-ticket or per-AWB, and shipper-facing sustainability claims require verifiable SAF accounting. The regulation explicitly frames aviation fuel as "a substantial share of aircraft operators' costs," establishing the cost-transmission mechanism that connects fuel regulation to air freight rates. *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 5, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng.

---

**MONITORING**

The regulation's operative articles require the European Commission to adopt delegated and implementing acts to operationalise the SAF blending mandate, reporting obligations, and verification framework. *Analytical inference:* Based on standard EU legislative timelines for implementing acts under transport regulations, these acts would be expected within 12–24 months of the regulation's entry into force (i.e., within 2024–2026). Whether they have been adopted, published, or are still pending as of this brief's generation date cannot be confirmed from the provided source blocks.

*Specific [delegated act adoption dates / implementing regulation publication dates] not available from primary sources as of 2026-05-27.*

The EASA digital reporting tool page (https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/environment/refueleu-aviation-digital-reporting-tool) was last updated 08 April 2026 per the page title captured in the source block, indicating active regulatory activity. *Source: EASA ReFuelEU Aviation Digital Reporting Tool page, EASA, last updated 08 April 2026. https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/environment/refueleu-aviation-digital-reporting-tool. The substance of that update is not available from the source block content provided.

Re-check window: Q3 2026 — retrieve the EASA digital reporting tool page in full and the DG MOVE ReFuelEU Aviation page to confirm implementing act status and reporting format publication.

---

**COST ALERT**
Verify that air carrier contracts and rate structures contain transparent SAF surcharge or SAF cost pass-through language. The regulation's SAF blending obligations on fuel suppliers and aircraft operators will translate into cost increases on air freight lanes departing EU airports. The mechanism is stated in the regulation: "Higher aviation fuel prices translating directly into higher end-consumer fares would reduce the connectivity of regions, the mobility of citizens and the competitiveness of the air transport sector." *Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2405, Recital 5, European Parliament and Council, 31 October 2023. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2405/oj/eng. The workspace, as a buyer of air freight capacity, faces pass-through exposure on every EU-departing shipment. Action: audit current carrier agreements for SAF surcharge clauses; quantify exposure per lane before the next contract renewal cycle.

**MONITORING**
Commission delegated and implementing acts required under the regulation to specify reporting formats, accounting methodologies, and verification procedures are pending or may have been issued after the source block capture date. Until those acts are retrieved and reviewed, the workspace cannot confirm the full scope of documentation it may be required to produce or pass upstream. Re-check window: Q3 2026 (see Anticipated Authoritative Guidance section).

**MONITORING**
*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, acting as freight forwarder arranging air shipments on behalf of shippers, bears any direct compliance obligation under ReFuelEU Aviation (as distinct from obligations borne by aircraft operators and fuel suppliers) requires counsel review of the operative articles, which are not fully available in the provided source blocks.
